author: NoticiasALB
title: [Manresa] Propuestas para prevenir las violencias (al hilo del asesinato de Carles, la criminalización racista en redes y la detención de sus asesinos)
content:
ALB. Noticias-

 A continuación traducimos el texto de A l'Aguait de Manresa, campaña que trata sobre la seguridad desde un punto de vista comunitario, a fin de combatir la histeria securitarista que invade la sociedad cada verano, gracias a noticias y sucesos desagradables que tienen que ver con actos delincuenciales y criminales. Esta vez el suceso ha escalado de gravedad, habiendo un

asesinato

. De aquí se lanzó una amplia campaña por redes sociales criminalizando a todos los jóvenes de origen marroquí de la ciudad. La extrema derecha agitó todo lo que pudo hasta que apareció uno de los supuestos perpetradores, que es de origen catalán. Dejando a un lado que se les cayera el argumento, la ultraderecha utiliza estos sucesos de forma habitual y la sociedad va exigiendo medidas "duras", policiales y represivas, antes que luchar contra las causas sociales primeras que originan estas bombas de relojería adolescente. Así pues, el llamdo "Movimento Popular de Manresa" se movilizó y presentó su propuesta, que os la copiamos aquí debajo: 


El orginal, en catalán

. 


Desde A l'aguait, proceso popular de seguridad comunitaria en Manresa y desde el Movimiento Popular de la ciudad,

asumimos nuestra responsabilidad

, como colectivos que trabajamos de forma comunitaria en la ciudad,

de aportar análisis y propuestas útiles

, que nos permitan pasar de la legítima indignación y la tristeza a trabajar por una ciudad

sin violencias, discriminaciones ni desigualdad

.


Estas políticas públicas y comunitarias, divididas en tres fases, surgen del trabajo que llevamos a cabo desde hace más de una década en las calles de Manresa, y del apoyo y las conversaciones con educadoras y expertas en ámbitos como la intervención con jóvenes, la educación y el trabajo social, las drogodependencias, la salud mental y la justicia restaurativa o la violencia juvenil. Están también basadas en la evidencia criminológica y en aprendizajes recogidos en todo el mundo a la hora de combatir la violencia interpersonal, social y comunitaria, especialmente entre jóvenes y desde los jóvenes.


Como Movimiento Popular,

nos preocupa el aumento de las violencias sociales, de los discursos de odio y de la deshumanización en los últimos años

, que sin duda están generando consecuencias materiales, en forma de más exclusión, una peor convivencia y un aumento del miedo entre la ciudadanía.

Un miedo que puede afectar a cómo las manresanas ocupan el espacio público

 y, por tanto, a la cohesión social, y dar alas a aquellos que se aprovechan y arañan votos deformando y distorsionando la realidad para hacernos maleables.

 En Manresa hay violencias que debemos combatir y transformar, aunque sea una ciudad segura.

Del mismo modo que confrontamos la violencia institucional, tampoco podemos ni queremos aceptar que haya personas que son víctimas directas de violencias en nuestra ciudad.


Es necesario, pues, poder

pensar serenamente qué está pasando

, cuál es el alcance de la problemática, cuáles son sus causas y, por tanto, todas las dimensiones que hay que abordar

para prevenir y trabajar en posibles soluciones

. Si algo queda claro, y solo hay que ver lo que ha pasado en otros momentos y contextos, es que abordar la violencia social y comunitaria como una problemática únicamente de seguridad, clamando ciegamente por endurecer uno de los códigos penales más duros de Europa, ni es útil ni ha sido una solución para reducir estas violencias, que tienen múltiples causas.


En el centro, tienen que haber políticas que rompan con las viejas recetas de siempre, que no han sido útiles para disipar la sensación de miedo. Y que no han reducido ni la desigualdad económica, ni la exclusión social, ni la segregación racial, el machismo y la LGTBIfobia, las adicciones y el sufrimiento psíquico o la infravivienda, que siguen creciendo y generando un caldo de cultivo que es imposible de atender desde el punitivismo.


Al mismo tiempo, es urgente incorporar a cualquier análisis la dimensión de género, especialmente en lo que respecta a los mandatos de masculinidad hegemónica que recaen sobre los chicos. En barrios atravesados por el desposeimiento económico, donde las vías tradicionales de inserción y reconocimiento social están bloqueadas, la necesidad de "demostrar que eres un hombre" es un factor de riesgo determinante. Las administraciones deben entender que la violencia, la falta de empatía y las conductas altamente autodestructivas no son innatas, sino la …

author: Redaktionsgruppe To Dialytiko
title: Eine Kritik der dekolonialen Ideologie
content:
Der folgende Text ist der Vortrag, den die Redaktionsgruppe der Zeitschrift ‘To Dialytiko’ im Rahmen der dreitägigen Veranstaltungsreihe „3 Tage zu Krieg, Nationalismus und anderen Übeln, 24.–26. Oktober“ hielt, die von der Gruppe ‘RevDef’ im besetzten Haus „Fabrika Yfanet“ organisiert wurde.


Die Faszination der „dekolonialen Theorie“ in einer Zeit ideologischer Verwirrung


In den letzten Jahren hat der Diskurs über „Dekolonialisierung“ in akademischen Kreisen und sozialen Bewegungen eine zentrale Rolle eingenommen und wird als neue, radikale Sprache der Emanzipation präsentiert. Seine Wirkung ist unbestreitbar. Indem sie einen Rahmen für die Kritik am sogenannten „weißen“, „westlichen“ Blick als universelle Art der Weltdeutung bietet, übt diese Bewegung eine starke Anziehungskraft aus. Ihr Begriff „Dekolonialisierung“ ist zu einem Sammelbegriff geworden, der auf jeden Bereich anwendbar ist – von Hochschullehrplänen und Museen bis hin zu Ernährungsgewohnheiten und persönlichen Beziehungen – und verspricht, die vom Kolonialismus hinterlassenen Unterdrückungsstrukturen zu beseitigen.


Es ist jedoch von entscheidender Bedeutung, von vornherein klarzustellen, dass der hier untersuchte Begriff der „Dekolonisierung“ nicht mit dem historischen, politischen und militärischen Prozess des Zerfalls kolonialer Reiche verwechselt werden darf. Dieser historische Zyklus, der nationale Befreiungskämpfe umfasste und in der formellen Unabhängigkeit der ehemaligen Kolonien als Nationalstaaten gipfelte, war in den 1970er Jahren weitgehend abgeschlossen. Im Gegensatz dazu hat die heutige Verwendung des Begriffs eine fast ausschließlich metaphorische, kulturelle und erkenntnistheoretische Bedeutung angenommen, die Gegenstand dieser Kritik ist.


Der Aufstieg dieser Theorie lässt sich nicht losgelöst von ihrem breiteren historischen Kontext verstehen. Ihre Verbreitung fällt zeitlich mit der Schwächung und dem Niedergang proletarischer Kämpfe und Bewegungen auf fast der ganzen Welt zusammen und steht in einem kausalen Zusammenhang damit. Die Schwächung der proletarischen theoretischen und praktischen Kritik ging einher mit der Verstärkung geopolitischer, ethnokultureller, irrationalistischer und identitätsbasierter politischer Tendenzen und Ansichten, die bereits innerhalb sozialer Kämpfe vorhanden waren. Die dekoloniale Theorie als Inbegriff dieser „ethnokulturellen Wende“ innerhalb der Linken und des antiautoritären Milieus ist nicht bloß eine neue akademische Modeerscheinung, sondern ein Symptom einer tief verwurzelten politischen Niederlage. Ihre konzeptionellen Ursprünge liegen in der „kulturellen Wende“, die ab den 1970er Jahren die Sozialwissenschaften erfasste – ein Wandel, der selbst der theoretische Ausdruck des Niedergangs der alten Arbeiterbewegung war.


Diese Verlagerung von den sozialen Beziehungen der (Re-)Produktion hin zu Kultur und Wissenssystemen als eigenständige Sphären bildet den Kern der in diesem Beitrag dargelegten Kritik. Die dekoloniale Theorie verzichtet ausdrücklich auf die Kritik an der kapitalistischen Universalität und ersetzt den Klassenkampf – die grundlegende Triebkraft des historischen Wandels, die aus den Widersprüchen des Kapitalismus selbst hervorgeht – durch einen „externen Impuls“ von Subjekten, die kulturell und geografisch definiert sind. Dabei wendet sie starr analytische Gegensätze an (Westen/Nicht-Westen, Weißsein/Nicht-Weißsein), die komplexe soziale Realitäten übermäßig vereinfachen und zu reaktionären Positionen führen.


Ausgehend von den kritischen Analysen von Neil Larsen und Ross Wolfe [1] werden wir versuchen, die entscheidenden Fragen anzugehen, die von den Genossen von revdef aufgeworfen wurden. Wir werden uns bemühen zu zeigen, dass die dekoloniale Wende trotz ihrer radikalen Selbstdarstellung aus der Perspektive der Entwicklung einer antagonistischen Bewegung gegen Kapital und Staat negative Folgen hat und in reaktionäre politische Sackgassen führt.


Part I: Neil Larsens Kritik am „Jargon der Dekolonialität“


Im Zentrum der marxistischen Kritik an der dekolonialen Theorie, wie sie in den Arbeiten von Neil Larsen nachdrücklich zum Ausdruck kommt, steht die Aufdeckung einer grundlegenden Verfälschung: die Ersetzung der Analyse des Kapitalismus als vorherrschender Produktionsweise durch dessen Beschreibung als kulturelles Projekt. Larsens Analyse, inspiriert von Adornos Werk „Der Jargon der Authentizität“, konzentriert sich auf den führenden Vertreter der Bewegung, Walter …

author: Mahbub Abdillahi
title: Somalia’s uncertain hand-off
content:
This week, the Federal Government of Somalia held a domestic security conference in Mogadishu, attended by senior government officials and representatives of the international community. The conference came at a particularly critical time, as Somalia faces a growing dilemma on multiple fronts — the gradual drawdown of the AU mission in the country, the expected closure of international support structures, and an increasing political deadlock between the federal government and some federal member states.

These issues have been compounded by another concern that has grown over the past several months — the continuing threat posed by al-Shabaab and questions over whether the Somali National Army has the capacity to fill the

security vacuum

 that could emerge as African troops are reduced. However, the federal government is projecting far greater confidence in Somalia’s ability to manage the transition than many of its international partners anticipated.

Speaking at the conference, National Security Adviser to President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Aweys Haji Yusuf, who is also regarded as an influential presidential ally, said the withdrawal of international missions from Somalia was “the result of a long-term process” rather than a sudden decision. He noted that discussions and “assessments of Somalia’s ability to take greater control” of its own affairs had been underway for more than four years. According to Aweys, the government sought to determine when Somalia would be able to reduce its dependence on the UN, with assessments concluding that Somali institutions were increasingly capable of managing political and governance responsibilities that had previously received substantial UN support.

Somalia’s Minister of Religious Affairs and Endowments, Mukhtar Robow, who previously served as a senior figure in the militant group al-Shabaab before defecting, also addressed the gathering. Robow said Somalia’s security environment had “changed significantly,” adding that the country was now in a stronger position than it was in previous years.

The comments come amid increasingly assertive statements from President Hassan Sheikh’s administration that Somalia is preparing to assume greater responsibility for its own security and governance. Speaking at the Hananbure military training centre in Galgaduud during the graduation of thousands of new Somali National Army recruits, President Hassan Sheikh said international partners had played an important role in supporting Somalia’s fight against a prolonged insurgency, but stressed that reliance on foreign forces could not continue indefinitely.

Somalia is entering one of the most consequential reductions in international support since outside powers began rebuilding the country’s security and political institutions more than two decades ago. Two processes are now unfolding simultaneously. The

United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS)

, the political mission that succeeded

UNSOM

, is due to cease operations on October 31, 2026, completing a two-year transition requested by the Somali government in the name of greater national ownership. Its responsibilities — including support for constitutional reform, elections, human rights, the rule of law, security-sector development, and the coordination of international assistance — are being transferred to Somali institutions, the UN Country Team, and other partners.

Separate from that process, however, is an increasingly acute crisis surrounding the nearly 12,000 African troops deployed under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). Those forces depend heavily on the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) for much of the infrastructure that allows them to operate, including food, water, fuel, aviation, medical evacuation, communications, equipment support, and troop transportation. The convergence of the UN political mission’s closure with growing uncertainty over the future of this logistical system means Somalia could lose layers of international political and security support within months of each other, even as al-Shabaab retains a substantial presence across southern and central parts of the country.

The most serious shock has come from Washington. On July 1, Reuters

reported

, citing a US diplomatic note, that the Trump administration had informed the AU that it would no longer support UNSOS beyond the end of 2026 and would oppose a Security Council mandate continuing …

author: ROAPE
title: African migrant workers who cannot return
content:
Somebody in Kampala or Accra or Harare sees a job advertisement. Customer service, or something in IT, somewhere abroad. The pay is better than anything available at home. The recruiter is responsive and reassuring. A ticket arrives.


That is where most accounts of migrant labour abuse begin, and it is worth sitting with how ordinary it sounds. Nobody in that story is reckless. They are doing what people have always done when opportunity is scarce, which is to go where the work is.


What happens next is the part that does not make the news often enough.


The scale is global, not exclusively African.

UNODC, citing INTERPOL, reports

 that people from 66 countries across every continent have been trafficked into online scam centres, with 74 per cent of identified victims brought to centres in Southeast Asia. African workers are therefore one part of a much wider labour pool. Their experience still deserves particular attention because, as the cases below show, rescue does not end the problem when consular support and repatriation capacity are uneven.


The mechanism that makes everything else possible


Across the Gulf, Jordan and Lebanon, migrant workers live under a

sponsorship regime

 that ties a person’s legal right to remain in the country to one specific employer. That employer can, in practice, determine whether the worker changes jobs, and in some cases whether they can leave the country at all.


It is lawful and it is routine, which is precisely why it deserves more attention than it gets. It does not require anybody to break the law to produce misery. It only requires an employer willing to use the leverage the system hands them. The result is a worker who cannot walk away, and once a person cannot walk away, everything else becomes negotiable: their wages, their hours, their passport, their safety.


The most extreme version of that principle is not lawful at all. Along the Thai border near Myawaddy, and in Shan State near the Chinese frontier, thousands of people are held in fortified compounds and forced to conduct online fraud for transnational criminal networks, targeting victims around the world through investment, romance, cryptocurrency and other scams.


A

United Nations report

 published earlier this year documented what that involves: torture and other ill-treatment, sexual abuse, forced abortions, food deprivation and solitary confinement. Survivors interviewed for it came from Ghana, South Africa and Zimbabwe, among other countries. One man from Ghana described being made to watch a friend beaten in front of him.


The legal system and the criminal one are not equivalent, and nobody serious claims they are. But they run on the same principle: take away a person’s ability to leave, and there is very little they can refuse.


Rescue is not the same as return


There is a further problem that receives almost no attention. Crackdowns can close individual sites without dismantling the wider networks, which have

repeatedly adapted, relocated or expanded elsewhere

. And the people pulled out of them are frequently left in limbo.


Reuters reported in March 2025

 that nearly 7,000 people rescued from scam centres in Myanmar were awaiting repatriation through Thailand, including Chinese, Indonesian and African nationals. Some remained in militia-run border camps facing food shortages, limited medical care and no means to pay for the journey home. That imbalance matters: rescue can happen in one day, while return depends on documentation, diplomatic coordination and a government able to act for its citizens.


This is what makes consular capacity a human rights issue rather than an administrative one. Being rescued and being home are two different things, and the gap between them is measured in whose government showed up.


Saad Kassis-Mohamed has spent years arguing that these are not isolated tragedies but predictable outcomes of systems working as designed. His advocacy has focused on migrant-worker protection, humanitarian action, climate justice and social equality, and on a demand that sounds modest until you try to enforce it: that reforms should be judged by whether anything actually improved for the people they were written for.


He develops that argument further in

The Kafala System

, prepared by Saad Kassis-Mohamed Center, which examines sponsorship-based dependency in the Gulf and Lebanon before extending the analysis to trafficking and forced criminality in Myanmar. The Center …

author: Francis Omondi
title: Reclaiming the Church’s Prophetic Voice: An Insider’s Take
content:
Kenya is in political angst.


Public confidence is at an all-time low. Political violence is spreading. Youth frustration is growing. Those entrusted with leadership are detached from the daily struggles of ordinary people. In such moments, society inevitably turns to one institution that has historically spoken when other voices fell silent: the Church.


Yet a debate has emerged. Some politicians, like Hon. Nelson Koech, MP, insist that the Church should stay away from politics and focus on prayer. Others, including Hon. S.K. Musyoka, the opposition leader, urge the Church to speak more boldly. The question is not whether the Church should involve itself in partisan politics. It should not. Does the Church have a public responsibility beyond worship and prayer?


The answer is yes. It does.


The Church has a prophetic vocation. That vocation obligates it to speak when justice is threatened, when power is abused, and when human dignity is violated.


Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, the former Chief Rabbi of the Commonwealth, observed that the fundamental concern of the prophetic tradition is with equality and a critique of the abuse of power. The biblical prophets consistently defended the poor and challenged rulers who oppressed the vulnerable. Prophecy was never merely about predicting the future. It was about telling the truth in the present. This was exemplified by the likes of Archbishops David Gitari, Ndingi Mwana a Nzeki, and Bishops John Okulu and Alexander Muge, among many Kenyan clerics.


Kenya’s current circumstances demand precisely such a voice.


Walter Brueggemann, in The Prophetic Imagination (1978), identifies three central tasks of prophetic ministry. The first is to tell the truth in a society that lives in illusion. The second is to grieve in a society that practices denial. The third is to express hope in a society tempted by despair. These are not political tasks in a partisan sense. They are moral and spiritual responsibilities.


Today, Kenya needs truth.


Citizens are increasingly concerned about corruption, state violence, economic hardship, and the erosion of public trust. The Church cannot honestly witness these realities and remain silent. Silence in moments of injustice is not neutrality. It is surrender.


Yet speaking prophetically is not the same as pursuing political power.


The Church is not called to govern the state. Nor is it called to endorse parties or candidates. Its role is different. It serves as the conscience of society. It reminds leaders that political authority exists to serve the common good and not private interests.


This distinction is important.


Canon Chris Sugden, of the Oxford Centre for Religious and Public Life, argues that bishops are fundamentally pastors and overseers. Their primary responsibility is to teach, pray, guard the faith, and strengthen the Church. The detailed translation of Christian convictions into political and social action often belongs to believers working within society itself.


Even so, this does not relieve church leaders of their public responsibility.


Joseph Ratzinger, later Pope Benedict XVI, in Church, Ecumenism, and Politics, argued that the Church must educate society by forming consciences. Its task is to cultivate openness to truth, justice, and moral responsibility. According to Ratzinger, the Church helps maintain the delicate balance between freedom and tyranny by shaping citizens who act according to conscience.


This means the Church cannot retreat into the private sphere.


Political power always carries the temptation to elevate itself above moral accountability. Every government, regardless of ideology, requires institutions capable of reminding it that it is not absolute. The Church performs this function when it speaks from moral conviction rather than political interest.


Unfortunately, Kenya’s churches have not always fulfilled this role consistently.


Many citizens perceive a troubling pattern. Church criticism of government often appears louder when political opponents are in power and quieter when allies occupy State House. Different denominations have sometimes adjusted the volume of their prophetic witness according to their proximity to political influence. Such inconsistency weakens public confidence and undermines moral authority.


This problem is not unique to Kenya.


Reflecting on post-apartheid South Africa, Allan Boesak, in the essay “The Future of Prophetic Christianity” (1993), warned that …

author: Christopher Rutledge
title: Free speech is not freedom from facts
content:
A strange thing happens to a claim when it moves from a WhatsApp group or a Facebook post into a radio studio. It changes its clothes.


What begins as a rumour on social media can sound very different once it enters a national broadcaster’s studio. The familiar presenter, the recognised station, the rituals of a professional interview, and the authority of being on air all lend the claim credibility it didn’t have before. The listener is no longer hearing merely what someone said online; they are hearing it through an institution they have been taught to trust, and it is easy to assume that if it has reached the microphone, someone must have checked whether it is true.


That is why the recent Broadcasting Complaints Commission of South Africa

(BCCSA) ruling against SAFM

 matters. It is also why some of the criticism of the ruling misses the point.


After SAFM broadcast the apology ordered by the BCCSA, some people asked whether organisations such as Macua (Mining Affected Communities United in Action) were now deciding what could and could not be said in the media. Others suggested that this amounted to controlling the narrative or restricting free speech.


It sounds like a reasonable concern. Nobody should want civil society, government, business or any political organisation to decide which opinions South Africans are permitted to hear.


But that is not what happened here.


We did not ask SAFM to stop interviewing Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, nor did we ask the broadcaster to ban March and March, nor did we ask that controversial views about immigration be removed from the public conversation.


What we were asking was fairly basic: if a claim is presented as fact, particularly on a national broadcaster, the audience is entitled to know what it rests on and whether it can be verified.


The lie about immigrants and crime


Ngobese-Zuma told SAFM listeners that foreign nationals were responsible for 60% of serious crime in Gauteng… Read that sentence again. Not that she believed migrants were contributing to crime. Not that immigration was, in her view, badly managed. She gave a figure: 60%.


A number sounds precise; it sounds researched and official. Once such a number is repeated on national radio, it begins to circulate.


People repeat it at work. Someone forwards it to a WhatsApp family group. A politician quotes it. A Facebook post appears, saying, ‘Even the radio said foreigners commit 60% of crime’.


Soon, nobody remembers where the figure began. They only remember the figure.


However, when the claim was examined, the evidence failed to support it.


GroundUp


and the

Institute for Security Studies

 investigated the broader claims about migrants and serious crime and found no evidence that foreign nationals account for anything approaching such a share of serious crime. Even the prison statistics commonly invoked in these debates do not tell the story people imagine: a significant proportion of foreign nationals in prison are there for immigration-related offences, not the violent crimes usually implied.


And this is the crucial point: saying that a police officer mentioned a figure does not magically make it a reliable statistic, especially since it has been debunked numerous times.


Anti-immigrant, ‘peaceful’ protesters in Alexandra, Johannesburg, carrying weapons and some covering their faces. File photo by Simon Ramapuputla


The BCCSA found that SAFM failed to inquire about the claim’s origins. The commissioner noted that the presenter neither endorsed the 60% claim nor challenged it, leaving listeners to accept it.


That is the distinction between censorship and journalism. Censorship says: you may not say that. Journalism says: you have said it; now show us why we should believe you.


The lie about foreign military bases


The distinction matters because the 60% claim was not the only one. Listeners were also told about foreign military bases allegedly operating in South Africa. They heard allegations that NGOs receiving foreign funding were buying weapons. There were claims that explosives were entering the country and that foreigners were paying police officers.


Again, these are not vague political opinions. Either the military bases exist or they do not. Either particular NGOs are buying weapons or they are not. Either there is evidence of a widespread system in which migrants bribe police officers or there is not.


When

GroundUp

 examined some of these claims, the picture began …

author: Siddharth Akali
title: Mineral Beneficiation: A Pipedream of Prosperity in an Unequal Financial Architecture
content:
Since 2023,

14 African countries

 have introduced

export restrictions

on unprocessed critical minerals, requiring “local beneficiation” – or in-country processing and manufacturing – prior to export, and demanding technology and financing.


Wealthier countries are also supporting the idea of local beneficiation and stepping up investments in resource-rich countries, promising this will help to lift them out of poverty. Behind these promises, however, they are perpetuating a top-down, economic model that only serves their own interests, and are reducing long-standing equity-based claims for climate justice and reparations from the Global South to a business opportunity.


Promoted by Western governments and executed through their development banks and corporations, this model pushes African countries further into debt, allows wealth to flow out through tax avoidance, and imposes policy changes that undermine environmental and human rights, while diverting scarce public resources away from hospitals, schools and social protection.


Geopolitical interests at stake


Currently, China is one of the world’s largest producers and suppliers of critical minerals,

controlling over 80 % of the rare earth element supply

. In response, Western nations in the

G7

 and their allies – who need to

secure access

 to minerals for their growing energy,

digital

 and

military

 industries – are trying to

reduce their dependency on China

 and stepping up investments in the mining sector across the Global South.


Amidst these geopolitical tensions, multilateral development banks (MDBs) are increasingly being used as a tool to advance Western government interests. In May 2026, the World Bank Group announced it “

will quintuple support to the sector in the next five years

”, while the African Development Bank is working to make

critical minerals beneficiation central to Africa’s industrialisation

.


Imider silver mine in Morocco. Credit Lorena Cotza


Development banks are mobilising support for mining and beneficiation in three main ways. Firstly, identifying and designing projects that can fit into global supply chains and are profitable for the private sector. Secondly, providing host governments loans to

absorb risks from the private sector

 through

public private partnerships

, and set up the associated energy and transportation infrastructure. Thirdly, under the guise of providing “technical assistance” as well as the conditionalities attached to loans, MDBs end up acting as

shadow governments

 and pressure African governments to make industry-friendly reforms, including measures to fast-track projects.


A promise based on false assumptions


MDBs are opportunistically presenting critical minerals as a golden development opportunity for Africa. Their promises of prosperity, however, are built on two faulty assumptions.


The first is that there is infinite demand for critical minerals. In reality, projected demand has been overblown, leading to overinvestment in production capacity. For example, global

manufacturing capacity for lithium-ion batteries

 is about two to five times greater than current demand, resulting in waste, overextraction, overproduction and lower prices. This suggests that mineral-rich countries will need to

increase demand domestically

, factoring in higher competition and reduced income for their products.


The second is that mineral-rich countries will be able to fund their essential social services and infrastructure through income from mining and beneficiation. However, debt servicing and the global tax framework (with business structures channelling profits to offshore investors) will likely suck up any economic value before reaching the marginalized communities who are facing poverty.


Unfair global tax and debt systems undermine public financing for development


MDBs have historically pushed for extractive industries to be

private sector-led

, leaving governments at the mercy of mega mining-corporations whose capital far exceeds the gross domestic product of many African countries. These corporations are pushing mining host governments

to compete with each other

 for more investments by reducing resource royalties, weakening environmental and social safeguards, and giving tax breaks to resource companies.


Significant portions of mining value continue to flow out as companies

shift their profits to tax havens

. Meanwhile the G7 and other wealthy countries

have …

author: Dina A. Mohamed
title: Beyond useless guilt and insatiable victimhood
content:
In 2018, my first year living in Amsterdam, studying for a master’s degree in the arts, I went to a museum to attend a performance by a group of queer artists addressing questions of injustice. The setting seemed familiar enough until one of the presenters announced that anyone who did not belong to specified “marginalized identities” should leave the room. They began reading a list of those identities aloud.


For a moment, I just listened, suspended, trying to locate myself in the list. Then it became clear: the list excluded non-queer, white people. I, therefore, “belonged.” I found that the category I best fit in was “woman of color,” a definition I had never once used for myself at that time.


I stayed. The conversation turned to safety in the Netherlands, to harassment and violence connected to skin color, gender identity, sexual orientation. The others spoke from experience I could hear but not share. Amsterdam, for me, had been something else entirely: quiet nights walking alone through streets I did not know, a strange lightness I had no name for yet. No one had stopped me. No one had read me by my color. I am not denying that such violence exists, only that it had not, at that point, been my story.


And so, I said nothing.


That moment stayed with me. It crystallized something I had been sensing since arriving in Europe: a pressure, felt everywhere in public discourse, to read every experience through the lens of identity. To locate yourself on a map drawn by others and then speak only from that location.


What unsettled me was not the artists’ choice to create a protected space. It was the underlying logic, one I kept encountering: in seminar rooms, in cultural institutions, in the language of activist circles. A logic by which identity is constructed entirely on the axis of oppression: one group over another, history compressed into a single narrative, and every human being assigned a fixed position within it. You are either a victim or a perpetrator. There is no third position. The space between is simply erased. 


When pain becomes a pass


When being a victim is the only position that confers moral authority, the only place from which you are permitted to speak without being immediately questioned or condemned, then victimhood stops being a condition and starts becoming a currency. And currency, by nature, is something people reach for.


But to understand why this happens so readily today, you have to look at the broader cultural atmosphere in which identity politics operates. 


We live, as sociologist Frank Furedi argued in

Therapy Culture:


Cultivating Vulnerability in an Uncertain Age

(Routledge, 2004), in a society that has undergone a profound redefinition of what a person is.

 Clinical language such as trauma, triggers, nervous system dysregulation, safe spaces and emotional damage has migrated out of the therapy room and into everyday speech, political discourse and social media. The effect is that vulnerability has become the defining feature of how people understand themselves and others. To be a person, in this framework, is first and foremost to be at risk, to be potentially harmed, to be in need of recognition for your wounds. The self is constituted around its injuries.


This matters because it explains the ease with which therapeutic self-diagnosis feeds into political victimhood. When the culture already teaches you to understand yourself primarily through the prism of what has damaged you, and when the cultural framework simultaneously grants moral authority only to those who have been damaged, the two systems reinforce each other seamlessly. It offers people a coherent identity, a community, a moral position and a language, all at once. What it does not offer, and what it actively erodes, is agency. Therapeutic culture places people in a permanent state of recovery rather than transcendence: you are instructed to acknowledge your wounds endlessly and to identify yourself with and through them. Applied to politics, this means suffering becomes not something to be overcome collectively but, in a twisted way, something to be performed and preserved because it is the source of your standing.


Philosopher

Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò

 put it plainly: “pain — whether borne of oppression or not — is a poor teacher. Suffering is partial, short-sighted, and self-absorbed. We shouldn’t have a politics that expects different: oppression is not a prep school”. This is a difficult thing to …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: The “Rape Tournament”: Online Humour and Normalisation of Rape Culture in Namibia
content:
Between April 2024 and February 2025, Namibia recorded

 4,405 cases


of gender-based violence (GBV), of which 1,345 were cases of rape. These figures may not reflect the actual prevalence, as many incidents, particularly in rural communities, remain unreported due to persistent barriers to reporting. The most recent shocking case happened in June when a


25-year-old

 woman was gang raped at knife point by nine minors aged between 15 and 17. The news spread widely across social media, and with it came a violent


discourse

.

 One might expect that such dark and painful news would spark empathy, outrage, and solidarity. Instead, the news was met with many jokes, victim-blaming, sexual objectification, and open mockery of the survivor. These online comments are not merely insensitive humour. It is a disturbing display of how sexual violence is normalised and reveals social evidence of a broader rape culture in Namibia.


When Rape Becomes a “Tournament”


The title of this article emerged

from w

hat unfolded in the Facebook comment sections where the case, in effect, turned into a “rape tournament.”  At the dawn of the news, Namibians on Facebook rephrased this incident from a crime to sports, competition, and masculine camaraderie. In

this

Facebook discourse, the 9 suspects lined up in the photo like a football team, sparking sports references. A significant proportion of users, predominantly male, mocked the incident, curious about who the

“man of the match”

 was and who

“kicked the first penalty”.

 They further referred to the assault as a

“round-robin tournament,”

all of which transformed this violent crime into a public spectacle. 


This discourse appeared to erase the criminal and dehumanising act and reduced the survivor’s trauma to jokes and entertainment. Thus, the “rape tournament” term is used deliberately not to sensationalise the crime, but to describe how many commenters collectively reframed gang rape as though it were a sporting event. These comments construct an entirely different narrative about the survivor and perpetrators. She is no longer portrayed as a survivor of violence. She is rather signified as a playing field upon which the “match” occurred. This, in turn, frames the perpetrators as players whose acts are evaluated, celebrated, and compared. This shows that the football jokes were not isolated comments but formed a pattern.  


The social media comment section acts as a cultural space in which violence is publicly rehearsed, reinforced and legitimised.


The humour masked the true horror of the assault. When rape becomes a tournament, it sustains the rape culture in Namibia. Sexual violence alone does not sustain rape culture; it is also fed by the everyday attitudes, language, and habits that excuse, downplay, or normalise these acts. At its core, these Facebook comments show exactly how humour is used as a tool to keep rape culture alive and well in online spaces.


Victim Blaming Masked as Safety Concerns


Victim-blaming

 rarely appeared in explicit form. It was masked as “safety advice,” in which commenters framed their responses as concern for women’s safety. A significant number of people questioned why she was out that late at night,

with

one male user cautioning all women to stay indoors as soon as the streetlights go on to protect themselves. Women were advised not to walk at night, not to make unnecessary movements after dark

.

 One female commenter even suggested that the survivor should have remained at the home of the man she had allegedly visited and simply endured the “walk of shame” the following morning. At face value, these comments appear protective. However, they subtly relocate responsibility from those who commit violence to those who experience it. The discussion therefore ceases to ask why boys assaulted a woman and instead asks why a woman was outside.


The safety of women in Namibia is a concern given the increasing GBV-related cases in the country. However, the Facebook discussion extended beyond safety concerns and focused predominantly on regulating women’s movements, clothing, relationships and behaviour while remaining largely silent on the conduct of the alleged perpetrators. This kind of talk just aims to control women instead of questioning violent and toxic male behaviour. The burden of preventing sexual violence was therefore relocated from those who commit it to those who experience it. This sheds light on the double standards on …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Faraaz Mahomed
title: Reading List: Faraaz Mahomed
content:
My novel,

Mother/Land

, focuses on a law professor, Salim, a South African in New York, who finds out that he is the product of an affair between his mother — Sawligha — and an apartheid politician. The story engages with the recent past as well as the apartheid years, telling parallel histories about the Fees Must Fall movement in South Africa, Black Lives Matter in the US, forced removals under the Group Areas Act, and the experience of a Muslim immigrant in New York with a gay Afrikaans brother whose life he might save.

Salim has a sunken world-weariness, which is perhaps rooted in his intellectualization and his provenance. There is no shortage of such protagonists wandering the streets of New York, whether in

Herzog

,

Open City

, or

Netherland

. Interestingly, two of these are also immigrant narratives, although the latter might not characterize itself as such. My own experience as a South African of Muslim origin living in New York certainly shaped the story, but I read

We Need New Names

 with great interest, and I found some of the complexities of Salim and his family in it.

The theme of inheritance is one of the most prominent in

Mother/Land

. Sawligha and Salim’s relationship is central, and this dialogue in the matrilineal relationship (and to some extent the patrilineal too) had me reaching for

On Earth We’re Briefly Gorgeous

 by Ocean Vuong and

The Return

 by Hisham Matar. These are beautifully gifted writers, not only in their prose, but also in the intimacy with which they write. Looking for intimacy, and for the ‘lostness’ that Salim conjures, I often turned to

In a Strange Room

 — a brilliant and relentlessly personal text.

Sawligha’s arc takes place during the days of the removals. Richard Rive’s

Buckingham Palace

 stood out as a reference text about District Six, but I think my own family history in Vrededorp/Fietas/Fordsburg/Pageview (a cluster neighbourhood in Johannesburg) was a good starting point too. To understand the topography and to build a reliable history of what was left of the district, I relied on Sean Field’s

Lost Communities, Living Memories

 and on

South African History Online

 (a great resource!). The story of Sawligha’s affair with an apartheid politician is pure fiction, but I’d decided that Carl Lamprecht, Sawligha’s lover and Salim’s father, would be a contemporary of DF Malan. I did not read up much on him (merely picking up facts from Wikipedia), but there are small details that have helped to tell the history, and indeed portray Carl as a multidimensional character.

To capture the perfect naïve goodness of Salim, and to engineer (as my editor Fourie likes to say) a version of a person who intellectualizes too much and yet finds himself ultimately wanting, I found something quite akin in

The Idiot

. The tragedy of it and the beauty of it are very much the stuff of my daydreams — and the bittersweetness of Dostoevsky is something I find really captivating, and has actually helped me write the voice of by far the wisest character in the novel — eight-year-old Aa’isha.

I struggled with Aa’isha, Salim’s daughter, who sees the intricacies of the world and endeavors to understand them, all the while feeling like the contradictions and the lies that adults tell themselves are utterly nonsensical. It was a creative growth path for me personally, and I spent an inordinate amount of time reading everything from

The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time

 to

The Girl with the Louding Voice

 to try (and very possibly fail) to get the words, the logic, the temperament, and the reality of Aa’isha right.

As a psychologist, I went back to Piaget and Erikson, but the truth is that I am under no illusions that the voice is marked by a precociousness that I couldn’t quite erase (and that, by the final edit, I had decided was just the right amount of weird, unreliable humanness). I think that’s part of the beauty of writing children, though — because they do turn out to be the most astute of characters, even when their vocabularies don’t quite match their insight.

Reading

Zuleika Dobson

 helped with the metaphysical aspects of my storytelling (Sawligha is, after all, a ghost), but I enjoyed telling the paranormal aspects with a recognition of their ambivalent relationship to reality. Olga Tokarczuk’s

House of Day, House of Night

 is mystifying, and Ben Okri’s

Famished Road

 trilogy contains beautiful stories about the ability to travel between …

author: ROAPE
title: Introducing ROAPE’s newest affiliate
content:
I consider myself an organic intellectual because of my revolutionary commitment to confronting injustice and grounding scholarship in the lives and struggles of ordinary people. That is why joining the ROAPE Editorial Working Group feels like finding an intellectual home. Questions of poverty, inequality, and maldevelopment have long occupied my intellectual imagination, shaping my interest in critical political economy— from Marxian and postcolonial political economy to social reproduction theory and racial capitalism. This rests on the understanding that global and local inequalities are not accidental or ahistorical, but products of historically constituted struggles over power, labour, resources, and social relations.


For me, political economy stretches our imagination beyond ivory-tower debates. Beyond the African context, it illuminates the precarious existence of the waiter whose livelihood depends on tips, the care worker whose labour sustains ageing societies, the refugee navigating insecure labour markets, communities bearing the disproportionate burdens of climate change, the doorman shivering through the cold winter, and even the invitation to round up a purchase for charity at a corporate checkout. These seemingly mundane encounters invite deeper questions about labour, value, power, race, inequality, and the distribution of resources.


These questions have shaped both my academic and professional journey. Before undertaking my PhD in Development Studies at SOAS University of London, I worked across academia, government consultancies, international development, and civil society activism. Those experiences reinforced my conviction that scholarship is most meaningful when it remains connected to the realities of people’s lives and contributes to wider struggles for justice. My doctoral research on tourism, labour, and social protection in The Gambia examined how global and state-administered neoliberalism shape the everyday experiences of precarious workers whose labour sustains one of the country’s key industries. More broadly, my research sits at the intersections of political economy, labour, social protection, and African development, with particular attention to how colonial legacies, global and racialised capitalism continue to reproduce inequality across the continent.


This commitment continues to inform my work beyond the academy. I recently founded Karantaa, a Pan-African Research and Policy Lab, to create a space where critical scholarship, public policy, and civic engagement intersect. Through Karantaa, I seek to contribute to the democratisation of knowledge production and advance epistemological decolonisation through rigorous research and engaged public scholarship.


As an Editorial Affiliate, I look forward to contributing to ROAPE’s collective intellectual and political project while learning from its remarkable community of scholars, activists, and practitioners. I hope my work contributes, however modestly, to a tradition of scholarship that is historically grounded, theoretically rigorous, politically engaged, and accountable to the lives and struggles of ordinary people.


The post

Introducing ROAPE’s newest affiliate

 appeared first on

ROAPE

.

author: Oyugi Abednego Ochillo
title: Whose Kingdom Is It? Religion and Power in Kenya
content:
In June 2026, Burkina Faso’s Transitional Legislative Assembly

passed a law

 giving the state new powers to license and monitor religious worship. Weeks later, Captain Ibrahim Traore told Burkinabe students studying Sharia in Saudi Arabia that they need not come home, framing the choice of what to study abroad as

a question of national loyalty

. A government that can suspend preaching and threatens someone’s citizenship over a course of study has decided that religious authority is, at bottom, a security problem, something to be licensed, monitored and disciplined from above.


Kenya is fighting a version of the same battle from the opposite direction, and from below rather than above. During the 2024 Finance Bill protests, young Kenyans

accused

 churches of accepting political donations while remaining silent as the state used force against demonstrators, and told clergy to return the money before expecting to regain anyone’s trust. Where Traore reached for a decree, Gen Z reached for a demand addressed straight at the pulpit. That is the more interesting fight, because it is being waged through persuasion and public shame rather than law, which makes it slower and messier, but also more honest about what accountability from a religious institution should actually look like. Burkina Faso is useful here only as the outer edge of what state control of religion can become. From here, this piece stays in Kenya.


My argument is that Kenya’s churches, particularly the Pentecostal and charismatic institutions that dominate the country’s religious economy, have built a financial and political relationship with the state that Gen Z is now the first generation to seriously question from inside the pews rather than from outside them. Paul Gifford’s scholarship explains the theology that made this relationship possible. William Ruto’s conduct since 2024 shows exactly how a sitting president exploits it. A small number of clergy and lay institutions are demonstrating, unevenly, what it would actually take to break the pattern.


The question Gen Z is actually asking is not abstract, and it deserves to stand largely in the protesters’ own words rather than mine. “I’m here because our country’s money is being misused,” one protester told reporters outside Jesus Winner Ministry in June 2025, days after President Ruto

donated

 twenty million shillings to that same congregation. Occupy Church’s own organizer,

Mwabili Mwagodi

, put the same challenge more bluntly to the churches themselves: “Where is this money coming from? Bring us the receipts.” Even some of the clergy have started to frame the comparison the same way. In his 2025 Ash Wednesday homily, Nakuru’s Catholic Bishop Cleophas Oseso

warned

 that congregations should not be seen accepting political donations while “schools have no books and hospitals have no medicine”. That was the actual framing of the question. Not a general complaint about corruption in the abstract, but a direct comparison between what a single Sunday donation cost and what an unfunded clinic or classroom costs the same week.


The economics of miracle and tithe


Harambee

 itself is not the problem. It began as a genuine communal practice, neighbours pooling money for school fees or a hospital bill, and much of it still works that way at the level of a village or a church congregation raising funds for a borehole. What changed is scale and direction. Once national politicians discovered that a

harambee

 podium could double as a campaign stage, the same word came to describe a president handing over millions of shillings in a single televised gesture, and the distance between those two things is most of what this argument is trying to name.


Paul Gifford’s decades of

research

 on Kenyan Christianity describe how the prosperity gospel replaced older forms of church accountability with a direct transaction between believer and preacher. A pastor promises breakthrough, healing, or business success. The believer gives, often well beyond what they can afford, because the sermon has recast giving itself as the mechanism of the miracle. The old model, where a congregation could hold a church leader to account because it funded him collectively, gets replaced by something closer to a bet. Gifford’s sharper point, the one that matters for this piece, is what that bet does to politics rather than to individual believers. Once poverty is read as a spiritual test rather than a policy failure, a …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘Like ICE’: Western Cape police accused of unlawfully detaining foreign migrants
content:
Up to 200 foreign migrants have been in detained by the police since the 30

th

 of June as part of the state response to the anti-immigration protests led by March and March and Operation Dudula. The Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration declared even before the xenophobic deadline that the arrest of “illegal foreign nationals” would be intensified.


The Western Cape Coalition Against Xenophobia (WCC-AX) is raising the alarm over the conduct of the South African Police Service in Robertson and surrounding towns, which it likens to that of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE) of the United States of America. ICE is is carrying out the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, often arresting migrants in public places and immigration offices. They have killed 8 immigrants and protesters this year, with over 50 detainees dying since 2025.


WCC-AX say that the rights of the migrants have been trampled upon as they languish in jail in Robertson and surrounding Winelands towns, denied medication, their basic sanitary requirements, and food. They are all from our neighbouring states, mostly Zimbabwe, and Malawi, Mozambique and Lesotho.


The Robertson police denied these claims and said food brought by relatives and supporters of the detainees has been allowed, but access has to be managed. “The station commander has confirmed that food brought by relatives is permitted, subject to a controlled process, and that visits are allowed but managed due to the large number of family members seeking access to detainees,” said the police.


But the police are not managing the acceptance of goods as it is arbitrary, with some police officers refusing and others being sympathetic to the plight of the detainees, WCC-AX responded. “The acceptance of goods,  including medication, has been totally arbitrary, with some police simply refusing to accept items, going so far as to say they ‘don’t care’, while other police have acknowledged this pattern and acted differently, but all entirely at their own discretion apparently.”


Sheriff Ramaobi, an activist in the area, confirmed that they were told that they cannot bring anything to the detainees. “One of our colleagues who visited one of the prison cells in Robertson asked these questions in terms of, can we bring medication or food supplies to our migrant brothers and sisters?  And it was denied. Other police stations, like McGregor and Montagu, strictly said that we’re not allowed. We are not allowed to give any support to the people that are incarcerated,” she said.


The police also deny that the detainees have been kept in jail illegally, saying that they have acted within the law and in cooperation with the Department of Home Affairs. “The foreign nationals detained for immigration-related purposes are dealt with in terms of the applicable legislation and in cooperation with the Department of Home Affairs, which is responsible for immigration administration and deportation processes,” said SAPS.


WCC-AX disputes this, saying that after they paid the admission-of-guilt fines, they were supposed to be released and not kept in jail for over two months. “If the police wanted to continue to detain them, they should have followed the administrative procedures laid down in s34 of the Immigration Act. The law states that people have to be told why they are being detained and what their rights are, including their right to challenge the deportation decision and to legal representation. Their continued detention must come before a court with them getting the opportunity to make representations. This did not happen. That’s why their continued detention is unlawful,” WCC-AX argues.


Anti-immigrant protesters outside the provincial legislature in Cape Town on the 30

th

 of June. File photo by Mzi Velapi


WCC-AX demands


The key demands of the Western Cape Coalition Against Xenophobia include the release of the detainees, for SAPS members to “stop acting like members of March and March (and ICE in the US)”, and act within the law.


The anti-xenophobia group is also calling for the suspension of police officers accused of failing to enforce the law and human rights violations, and that they must be subjected to an inquiry. The South African Human Rights Commission must also conduct an investigation. “The minister of home affairs must explain why his departmental officials conflate criminal and administrative proceedings in contravention of the Immigration Act,” …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Too many elders receive care outside Nunavut, NTI says
content:
Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. says long-term care for elders in the territory has been inadequate for years, an issue that John Amagoalik’s situation has brought “into sharp focus.”


But the association tasked with making sure promises made in the Nunavut Agreement — which Amagoalik helped negotiate — are kept isn’t saying whether it plans to help the revered leader live out his final days at home.


Before

coming

 back to Iqaluit in June, Amagoalik had been living at the Embassy West long-term care facility Ottawa. His loved ones raised money for his flight and some health care needs but said they were depending on the GN’s Health Department to fund Amagoalik’s care and housing needs in the long term. 


The GN said its policies prevent funding privately arranged in-home care and housing through its long-term elder care programming. Now, with money running out, Amagoalik might have to leave Iqaluit again.


“Too many Inuit elders, including unilingual Inuktut-speaking elders, continue to receive care outside the territory, separated from their families, communities, language and homes,” wrote NTI spokesperson Annie Thomlinson in an email to Nunatsiaq News on Sept. 3.


She was responding to questions about whether NTI planned to help Amagoalik, for whom the organization is currently providing a rental unit at reduced rent.


NTI declined requests for an interview with its president, Gloria Uluqsi.


Amagoalik,

revered by many as the “Father of Nunavut,” dedicated decades of his life to advancing Inuit rights.


He served as the executive director of the Nunavut Land Claims Project starting in 1974, and after 1993 he led the land-claims settlement process with NTI, following the ratification of the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act. From 1999 onward, he also chaired the Nunavut Implementation Commission, the 10-member organization which eventually became Nunavut’s government.


“We would love to sit with the Government of Nunavut, the Health Department and NTI to have a discussion about how we can make this work. The alternative is that he will be sent back to Ottawa or to Rankin Inlet,” said Mark Stiles, a friend of Amagoalik. “He doesn’t want to do that.”


Anne Crawford, who has also been advocating for the family and is a lawyer involved with the Pairijiit Tigummiaqtikkut Elders Society, says s

he believes it’s the Nunavut government’s responsibility to find a solution and that she’s not familiar with any policy that would prevent the GN from contracting a private care provider in Iqaluit the same way it does with southern providers, such as Embassy West.


“What they’re saying is, ‘We never got around to building the policy and financial structures that would let us do what you’re asking us to do,’” she said.


“They’re building a three-seater bus and then telling us they don’t have room on the bus,” she added. “You should build a bigger bus.”  


Nunatsiaq News requested an interview with Nunavut’s Health Minister,

Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster,

 to speak about the state of elder care in the territory, but the department sent a written statement instead.


There are care homes in Iqaluit and Arviat for those requiring lower to moderate levels of support, and ones in Cambridge Bay, Gjoa Haven, Igloolik and Rankin Inlet for elders with more complex needs, department spokesperson Charmaine Deogracias wrote. Only the care facility in Rankin Inlet provides care for those with the most complex needs. 


Work is ongoing to expand long-term elder care in the Qikiqtaaluk and Kitikmeot regions. 


“Until that capacity is operational, out-of-territory long-term care remains necessary when assessed needs cannot be met through services available in Nunavut,” Deogracias said in the email. 


Crawford said in Amagoalik’s case, the services are available. The family says monthly costs for his care and housing are about $16,000 per month.


NTI, meanwhile, told Nunatsiaq News it’s actively working with the GN so that more elders can receive around-the-clock medical care within the territory. 


“NTI has advocated for expanded after-hours home care services and is seeking updates on the outcomes of the GN’s home care review,” said

Thomlinson.


NTI has provided $15 million toward the renovation of care homes in Arviat, Gjoa Haven and Igloolik, she also noted, and has also provided $8 million to the

Pairijiit Tigummiaqtikkut Elders Society for the development of an independent living complex for elders.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Ottawa ends NunatuKavut process for recognition of Indigenous rights
content:
The federal government has ended NunatuKavut Community Council’s bid to be recognized as an Indigenous group with rights under Canada’s Constitution.


“Following careful review of the extensive information provided by the

NunatuKavut Community Council

 to support their section 35 rights claim, Canada has determined that the evidence submitted does not satisfy the court-established tests for Indigenous rights and title,” James Sinclair, spokesperson for Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, told APTN News.


Sinclair said the review of NCC’s claim “included consideration of updated submissions, internal historical and legal analysis, expert reviews, and discussions with NunatuKavut.”


According to the NCC, the group was informed of the decision in a letter from Crown Indigenous Relations. A Sept. 8 statement from the group said that its “Memorandum of Understanding (MOU),” was also terminated. That 2019 MOU with Canada was set up to explore what rights the NCC should have as an Indigenous group.


“This decision specifically concerns the assessment of section 35 rights,” Sinclair said. “It does not affect NunatuKavut’s ability to apply for federal programs, services and partnerships that do not depend on section 35 recognition.”


The NunatuKavut Community Council, formerly known as the Labrador Métis Nation and the Labrador Métis Association, represents some 6,000 people in south and central Labrador who claim they are Inuit and not included in the Nunatsiavut land claims agreement. NCC members aren’t recognized as Inuit by any other federally recognized, rights-holding Inuit collective, and their recognition by Ottawa has been opposed by the

Nunatsiavut Government

 (and

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami

), as well as the

Labrador Innu Nation

.


In its news release, NCC assailed a statement from the Nunatsiavut Government supporting Ottawa’s decision.


“It was shocking to learn that confidential information about the department’s decision regarding NCC and our people was released to another Indigenous group,” NCC wrote in its release. “NCC has had no time to adequately review the letter and understand its implications. This alone demonstrates the degree of complicity between the Government of Canada and other Indigenous groups in Labrador around our negotiations.”


The statement added, “It is appalling that the Minster of Crown-Indigenous Relations would bend to pressure from other Indigenous groups on the denial of our claim. NCC has not been treated fairly throughout this process, and the honour of the Crown has not been upheld.”


In its own news release, the Nunatsiaq Government (NG) applauded Ottawa’s decision.


“This decision brings long-needed clarity,” said NG President Johannes Lampe. “Inuit identity is not something that can be self-declared — it is affirmed by Inuit, grounded in our culture and history. Concluding this table is an important step toward ensuring our rights, as Inuit, are protected, respected and upheld.”


The statement added that the Nunatsiavut Government opposed Canada’s negotiations with NCC “from the outset in 2018,” and argued that the Nunatsiavut Government is the only representative of Inuit in Labrador. Of particular concern to NG is the potential for programs, rights, resources and opportunities intended for Inuit to be diverted to “unrecognized groups.”


“This decision represents an important step toward strengthening Inuit self-determination,” said Lampe, “and ensuring that our treaty rights are respected. We look forward to continuing to work with the Government of Canada and other governments to build a stronger future for our people and communities.”


Jodie Ashini, grand chief of the Innu Nation, said Ottawa made “a necessary and responsible decision.”


A statement from the Innu Nation noted that NCC had made four prior attempts — in 1991, 2003, 2013 and 2017 — to secure federal recognition as an Aboriginal rights-holding group under Section 35 of the Constitution.


“For many years,” Ashini said, “Innu Nation has raised serious concerns about decisions by the Government of Canada to include unrecognized groups and its potential consequences for the established Aboriginal and treaty rights of the Innu and other recognized Indigenous peoples, including Inuit represented by the Nunatsiavut Government.”

author: Truthout
title: Trump Admin Removes Slavery Context From Former Confederate Statue Site
content:
The revision comes as members of the Trump administration have indicated plans to restore the statue at the site.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The Trump administration has removed language critical of slavery from the site where a Confederate memorial once stood in Arlington National Cemetery.

The Confederate statue was taken down after Congress voted to remove it from the grounds in 2023. Upon the statue’s removal, a plaque was installed at the site putting the former monument into context, noting its revisionist history and its “nostalgic, mythologized vision” of the antebellum South.

In addition to replacing that plaque, the White House has indicated that it plans to reinstall the statue.

The statue was first placed at the cemetery in 1914, donated to the site by the United Daughters of the Confederacy. That period of the country’s history saw the installation of numerous statues reimagining the history of the Civil War and the South in general, often as an attempt to further embed white supremacist ideals in society.

The statue depicted an enslaved Black man dutifully following his enslaver into a Civil War battle, imagery that is often described as the “faithful slave” trope, which historians say has been used to falsely convey that enslaved people were content with their lives before the war. The statue also featured an enslaved Black woman, depicted as a “Mammy,” caring for a white child — a racist caricature that has long been used to whitewash the brutality and exploitation of slavery.

The marker where the statue once stood noted how the memorial had portrayed “highly sanitized depictions of slavery.” The Trump administration’s new marker recognizes the former monument’s placement but omits any references to slavery whatsoever.

In addition to removing the language from the former site of the statue, the Trump administration also removed an explainer from the Department of Defense (DOD) website.

“This narrative of the Lost Cause, which romanticized the pre-Civil War South and denied the horrors of slavery, fueled white backlash against Reconstruction and the rights that the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments (1865-1870) had granted to African Americans,” that explainer had previously read.

DOD Secretary Pete Hegseth indicated in 2025 that the old statue would be returned to its former spot at some point during President Donald Trump’s second term.

“It never should have been taken down by woke lemmings,” Hegseth said last year.

Stephen West, a Catholic University historian who noticed the new signage while visiting Arlington this past weekend, condemned the changes.

“I’m deeply disturbed by the removal of that language and by plans to restore the statue — especially because they’re of a piece with the censoring and slanting of history at other federal sites,” West said.

Civil rights attorney Areva Martin also blasted the decision to remove the historical explainers.

“Arlington National Cemetery just quietly rewrote the truth about a Confederate memorial. What Congress mandated by law is being DISMANTLED by an administration that never accepted it in the first place,” Martin wrote in a Bluesky post.

“This is not progress. This is a DELIBERATE betrayal,” Martin added.
