title: India’s Gen-Z Movement: Challenges Ahead for the Teachers and the Buddhist Way Forward
content:
The resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, Minister of Education, Government of India (a Gen-X person born between 1965–1980), has come as a shock, as it was considered impossible to get a resignation from any minister of the Narendra Modi-led NDA government from 2014 till now. However, the students of Gen-Z (born between 1997–2012, now in the age group 14–29) made it possible, along with the Millennials (born between 1981–1996), Gen-X, and Gen-Alpha (born between 2013–2020). The Gen-Z students would be mostly from class 10th onwards, and some may be working professionals as well. The protests (mostly) by Gen-Z have shown the other generations that they have accomplished something that other generations could not have achieved in the last 12 years (although the support of other generations cannot be neglected). The Gen-Z students would then have a new level of confidence when they go to their classes and interact with their teachers. However, without the right guidance to channel it properly, this surge of confidence can easily tip into an obdurate, impudent, and supercilious attitude, turning their outlook entirely quixotic. Therefore, the role of teachers, supervisors, universities, institutes, etc., would come into the picture, and they would have to face certain challenges. The challenges mentioned are not exhaustive; instead, they are suggestive.

The first challenge that universities/institutes (overall) and individual teachers as well would face is: Are the Gen-Z students going to listen (śravaṇa in Sanskrit—the first step of learning) to their teachers and universities? Are they going to follow the rules and regulations of the university/institute and maintain the decorum of the classes? Why I think this may be a challenge is because the Gen-Z students, with their creativity of language and presentation, have shut the mouths of many mainstream media channels and politicians, and have also astonished political scientists who never expected the occurrence of this nation-wide protest (if not in India, then at least not under the present government). These students have not been in the mood to listen to anything that has no bearing on the government’s accountability for the suicides of many NEET aspirants. This is understandable considering the seriousness of the issue. However, some videos have shown that students have hooted at the biased media channels, as they have been determined not to listen to anything from them.

The second challenge deals with humility and humbleness. Humility is an important aspect of learning. Learning results in humility (as said, vidyā dadāti vinayaṁ). Learning also results from humility—if I think that I am superior to others in terms of knowledge, how can I learn from others? I would then do whatever I think is fit according to ‘me’, even if that act disrespects someone. Are the Gen-Z students going to contemplate their continuous learning from life (manan in Sanskrit—the second step for learning), or would they feel supercilious? Are the Gen-Z students going to be in the disposition to learn from their teachers? Why I think this may be a challenge is because the Gen-Z students have already contemplated the inevitable consequences of the ruining of the country if the lacuna in education is not fixed. For this, they have raised their voice for their right to education, and thereby they have taught the world the peaceful management of crowds, connecting people, and leading a crowd. However, this same sense of achievement may let them feel that they know everything. It is also possible that they may not contemplate new learning, reflect deeply, or sharpen their arguments and creativity. Rather, they may take refuge in harsh and abusive language to assert their points, which has already been seen in the protests by some of the students. This aggression might block any novel and meaningful discoveries in their learning journey.

The third challenge is the continuity and culmination of the above two and deals with real-life experiences (nidhidhyāsana). The real-life experiences of unexpected events occur only when we listen to others and continuously contemplate them. Without that, we would continuously live in one set of habituated thinking caused by our external environments. But by continuously listening to others, like our well-wishers—teachers, parents, friends, etc.—and critics, we would be able to contemplate and improve our habituated practices. But without checks and balances …

author: Unknown
title: KCDP: At least 22 women were killed, 33 others died under suspicious circumstances in August
content:
At least 22 women were killed by men in Turkey in August. Another 33 women died under suspicious circumstances, according to the monthly report published on Wednesday by the We Will Stop Femicides Platform (KCDP). Since the beginning of the year, the organization has documented at least 197 femicides and 215 suspicious deaths.


The KCDP has been compiling its own data on femicides since 2010. According to the organization, one reason for doing so is that state authorities do not publish systematic statistics on femicides. The documentation is based on cases reported in the media as well as reports submitted directly to the platform.


Perpetrators mostly from women’s immediate circles


The figures for August once again show that the greatest threat to women often comes from men in their immediate circles. Nine of the 22 women were killed by their husbands. Two women were killed by former partners, one by her ex-husband, two by their sons and one by her father. In other cases, the perpetrators were acquaintances or other relatives. This means that 41 percent of the women killed in August were murdered by their husbands.


The locations of the killings also challenge the notion of the home as a safe space: twelve of the 22 women — 55 percent — were killed in their own homes. Three women were killed on the street, two in isolated locations and two in cars, while others were killed in a hotel, at their workplace or in another public place.


Firearms used in nearly two-thirds of cases


Fourteen of the 22 women — 64 percent — were shot dead with firearms. Three were killed with bladed weapons, two died after being thrown or falling from a height, one woman was burned to death and another was strangled. In one further case, the exact cause of death could not be determined. According to the KCDP, five of the killings were linked to decisions the women had made about their own lives. In one case, an economic motive was identified. In 16 of the 22 femicides, it has not yet been determined what pretext the perpetrators used for their actions.


The platform sees this in particular as a structural problem: “As long as it is not established by whom and why women were killed, legal proceedings are not conducted effectively, perpetrators are not given deterrent sentences, and preventive measures are not implemented, violence will continue to manifest itself in ever new forms,” the report stated.


‘It is not the women’s deaths that remain suspicious, but the truth’


The high number of unresolved deaths is particularly alarming to the KCDP. With 33 cases in August, the figure once again exceeded the number of killings recorded as femicides. Under the heading “It Is Not the Women’s Deaths That Remain Suspicious, but the Truth,” the platform cited, among others, the cases of Rojin Kabaiş, Gülistan Doku and Aysun Yıldırım.


Evidence secured too late, contradictions that were not adequately investigated, and the premature classification of deaths as suicides or accidents have hindered efforts to establish the truth and deepened impunity.


“No woman’s death must remain unresolved. Every suspicious death must be effectively investigated to determine whether male violence was involved,” the KCDP demanded.


At the same time, the report makes clear that existing protection mechanisms repeatedly fail to protect women from lethal violence. Several of the women murdered in August had previously experienced violence and threats or had obtained protective measures against the men who later killed them. The KCDP therefore calls not only for action after a killing has occurred, but also for the consistent implementation of effective protection and prevention mechanisms.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Legislative Aide of May Chin Disappears While Under Investigation for Corruption
content:
AN AIDE OF pan-Blue legislator May Chin has disappeared while under investigation for corruption charges. Specifically, Chin’s legislative aide, Chang Chun-chieh, was found to have disappeared after authorities detected a low-battery alert on his monitoring bracelet. Chin is an independent but caucuses with the KMT and is generally understood to be a pan-Blue politician.

Chang has not been found since. It is thought that Chang deliberately destroyed the monitoring bracelet in order to flee.

Chang was facing 16 years in jail. Chin herself faces 12.5 years in jail on the same charges. Chin’s downfall comes from the most common category of corruption case facing politicians: embezzlement of subsidies meant for legislative assistants. According to prosecutors, Chin passed off relatives as legislative assistants, defrauding taxpayers of 7.87 million NT.

Despite the fact that embezzlement of subsidies meant for hiring legislative aides is a common category of corruption case, KMT lawmakers introduced a bill in 2025 that would have eliminated the need for invoices for reimbursements for such subsidies. The bill was criticized as providing a blank check for corruption. Among those to react against the bill were legislative assistants themselves, including a number of KMT legislative assistants, who saw the bill as contributing to the negative social perception of their profession.

It is to be seen if the KMT invests political capital into defending Chin, with the KMT alleging in past years that other political corruption cases are simply the DPP targeting political opponents. Consequently, the KMT has defended politicians ranging from former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je of the TPP to Yilan county magistrate Lin Zi-miao. Indeed, Ko’s assistant also absconded to Japan with key information, rather than return to Taiwan in the course of his case, perhaps not so different than Chang. In the meantime, the KMT has alleged that it is, in fact, the DPP that is corrupt–including claims that the DPP’s interest in funding initiatives ranging from drones to renewable energy is only due to illicit links to such companies.

Nevertheless, as a pan-Blue politician, Chin has also sometimes faced allegations of being China-funded, true or not. It is somewhat surprising to see her apparent political downfall come over embezzling subsidies meant for legislative assistants. One notes that in a similar timeframe, the borough warden of Cingshan Borough in Tucheng, as well as the chairman of the Chinese Youth Cultural and Educational Art Exchange Association, have been sentenced for organizing and participating in trips to China intended to promote positive perceptions of China.

Such trips are conducted as part of China’s United Front efforts directed at Taiwan. It has only been in the past few years, however, that the Taiwanese government has taken action on such trips as violating laws against Chinese infiltration, as well as election procedures.

author: groundxero
title: Germany: why the AfD won in Saxony‑Anhalt – and what happens next
content:
The surge in support for the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) in a provincial election on Sunday was far worse than the country’s mainstream political parties had feared. The party came close to winning a majority of votes with 43.8%, while support for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU) imploded.


 


Ed Turner

,

Aston University


 


The results of Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state election on September 6 were far worse than feared for the country’s mainstream political parties. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came close to winning a majority of votes, with 43.8%. This was about 4% higher than polls had suggested.


 


Support for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU), on the other hand, imploded. It won 17.2% of the vote, down from 37.1% in 2021, performing substantially worse than predicted.


 


At nearly 78%, turnout was up substantially compared with 2021 – in a way that helped the AfD.

Analysis


suggests the growth in its support came mostly from former non-voters, joined by a substantial number of erstwhile CDU supporters.


 


The

polarised


nature of the election, with 41% of voters surveyed beforehand wanting an AfD-led government but 46% favouring one led by the CDU, had some surprising effects. One was that it flattered the social democratic SPD and the Greens.


 


Both the SPD and Greens received tactical support from CDU and Left Party voters to make sure they reached the 5% of votes required to win seats in the state parliament.


 


The AfD,

which had said

 it would only seek to govern if it had a majority, now has several paths to seeing its candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, elected as Saxony-Anhalt’s minister president. Most likely is a deal with the Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), a party that combines left-wing economic policies with conservative ones on topics such as migration.


 


On election night, the

BSW made clear

 it had “overlaps” with AfD positions in some areas and that it would be “completely undemocratic” for the AfD to be excluded entirely from government.


 


If this failed, some support from the CDU would be a further route. The election of minister president is a secret ballot, and several CDU MPs reelected on Sunday have a long history of

suggesting

 there should be more openness to working with the AfD.


 


Support across society


 


The

AfD did best

 in Saxony-Anhalt among working-class voters (59%), as well as those with a lower level of education (57%) and those who perceived their economic situation as bad (65%). But even among graduates (30%) and voters who saw themselves in a good economic situation (37%), the AfD performed respectably.


 


It also secured over 40% of support among all age groups apart from the over 70s (31%). So the AfD can really claim to be a

Volkspartei

 or “people’s party”, with support from across society, across the state.


 


By no means was this a single-issue election. Exit polls revealed immigration was

one motivating factor

 for AfD voters, with 91% of them agreeing with the statement that they “were very worried too many foreign people live in Germany”. But so too was concern with security and the economy.


 


There was also real dissatisfaction (66% of all voters) at the state government, which had been led by the CDU since 2002. But the standing of Friedrich Merz’ government in Berlin was worse, with 83%

taking the view

 it was insufficiently concerned with the problems of ordinary people. Just 20% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt trust it to

improve the country

 substantially in the coming years.


 


Accompanying these sentiments, which can be found across Germany albeit more strongly in Saxony-Anhalt and other eastern states, there is a strand of dissatisfaction particular to the east. Seventy-three percent of all voters in Saxony-Anhalt

believed

 easterners were still second-class citizens in many situations.


 


This view is taken by 83% of AfD voters. The AfD has been rather successful in mobilising grievances about reunification and some

nostalgia

 about the days of the communist East Germany.


 


Assuming the AfD does form a government, there will be close scrutiny of the extent to which it can implement its hard-right manifesto – and, indeed, whether it

confirms the view

 of German intelligence that the party is demonstrably “right wing extremist” in the state.

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Inmates remain detained beyond jail time over recording lapses
content:
MANILA — Some political prisoners may have already completed their sentences but remain behind bars because prison authorities failed to properly account for time credits required by law, according to Kapatid, a support organization of families and friends of political prisoners.


The group raised the issue during a dialogue with newly appointed Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) Chief J/Dir. Efren A. Nemeño on September 1 at the House of Representatives.


Hosted by ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio, the meeting brought together Kapatid spokesperson Fides Lim, Health Action for Human Rights officer Victoria Neri, Kabataan Party-list Rep. Renee Co, and BJMP officials to discuss concerns raised by political prisoners, their families, and human rights advocates.


Kapatid said the continued failure to integrate time allowances earned by prisoners while under BJMP custody into their official Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) records has contributed to prolonged detention and forced some inmates to seek costly legal remedies simply to secure their release.


For the group, the issue reflects more than a bureaucratic lapse.


It raises questions about whether prisoners are being deprived of liberty beyond what the law allows.


Years behind bars


At the top of Kapatid’s six-point agenda was the immediate computation, transmission, and integration of time allowances earned by 11 political prisoners currently under BuCor custody.


According to official BuCor records transmitted to Kapatid in May 2026, several of these prisoners have spent more than 20 years in detention.


The group said some prisoners’ credited service, including Good Conduct Time Allowance (GCTA), already amounts to between 31 and 35 years.


Republic Act No. 10592 expanded the GCTA system by allowing deductions from prison sentences for good behavior and participation in rehabilitation and educational programs.


Kapatid said official records still show zero credited time allowances earned during the prisoners’ previous detention under the BJMP.


The group argued that these missing credits prevent authorities from accurately determining whether a prisoner has already completed a sentence.


“These zero BJMP credits in official carpetas trap PDLs in a deep administrative limbo that directly causes illegal over-detention and exacerbates extreme congestion,” Lim said.


Kapatid said the omitted credits indicate that several prisoners may already have fully served their sentences and could be entitled to immediate release once the records are properly reconciled.


The group urged the BJMP to immediately transmit certified records of GCTA, Time Allowance for Study, Teaching and Mentoring, and other applicable credits for review by the joint BuCor-BJMP Management, Screening and Evaluation Committee.


It also called for an automated and mandatory inter-agency system that would ensure earned credits automatically follow a prisoner upon transfer from BJMP custody to BuCor facilities.


Paying for freedom


Kapatid said the failure to integrate prison credits has created another burden that falls most heavily on poor prisoners and their families.


Instead of receiving timely release evaluations, some detainees resort to filing petitions for habeas corpus to compel authorities to act on records that prison agencies should already be maintaining.


A writ of habeas corpus allows courts to determine whether a person’s continued detention remains lawful.


Kapatid argued that prisoners should not have to spend money on court proceedings simply to force agencies to perform responsibilities already mandated by law.


“PDLs should not have to go to court and pay for a habeas corpus petition simply to compel prison agencies to perform duties that the GCTA law, Republic Act 10592, requires them to perform,” Lim said.


The group described such petitions as anti-poor because many families already struggle to shoulder the daily costs of supporting detained relatives.


Those expenses often include food, medicine, transportation, and other basic needs that prisons do not adequately provide.


Kapatid cited one case in which a political prisoner paid a P40,000 down payment to a private lawyer to file a habeas corpus petition.


The family was reportedly expected to pay another P40,000 in succeeding fees, excluding appearance costs and documentary expenses.


Kapatid said it advised against the arrangement because the prisoner had already secured free legal …

author: rti_admin
title: India’s Unfinished Independence
content:
Every August 15, the flag goes up over the Red Fort, the anthem plays in every school and University for a day to celebrate being free. We call it Independence Day — the day India stopped being ruled by the British after two hundred years. And I celebrate it too. But every year, sitting with it a little longer than a headline or a holiday usually gets, one question won’t leave me. Free from what, exactly, and free for whom? The British extracted our wealth, silenced us, and treated us like subjects and inhumane instead of people. They eventually left. But did the thing they left behind actually go with them? Seventy-five-plus years later, many people are still living under a kind of threat, inhuman, and subject to no major change, and the political power is transferred from one hand to another. That time, foreign rule, and the present time, the elite and the oppressed class. caste, patriarchy, or social hierarchy systems- nobody ever really dismantled them, just handed them down like inheritance. The face in charge changed. For too many people, the situation underneath it didn’t. None of this is me rejecting the freedom we won or the people who died for it. It’s me refusing to let “freedom” become something we wave on a flagpole once a year without looking at who still doesn’t have it. After independence, many have hope for major change. We are ruling ourselves at least; nobody discriminates against us, but it is only theoretical, not practical.

We, the people of India, aren’t one religion. We’re not just Hindu, or just Muslim, or Christian, or Sikh — and the Constitution doesn’t lean on any of that in its opening line. It says: “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.” That’s a bigger sentence than it looks. India was never built to belong to one group. Many people are sacrificing their lives, their homes, their hope, their relatives, etc., every family, every tongue, every tradition, without asking anyone to give up who they are to be let in. The Constitution doesn’t just govern us. It protects the different ways we live, our culture, tradition, and language. But that raises a fair question: why does a free people need a document telling them how to live? If human beings are born free, shouldn’t that be enough on its own? For most of history, freedom on paper and freedom in real life were two completely different things. Before the Constitution, millions of people on this land weren’t fully recognized as human, and they were denied all human rights. No education, no right to object to injustice out loud, no fundamental rights. treated as animals; they were not counted as citizens. Two hundred years of British rule made all of that worse, and many people gave everything to end it. Even now, it’s worth asking: is that independence something everyone actually gets to feel, or is it still a promise some people are still waiting on? The Ambedkar Constitution is not just a rulebook. They wrote down a vision; it is a way of life, what Ambedkar called Prabuddha Bharat, an “Enlightened India” where every person could live with dignity and respect, no exceptions. A constitution isn’t a book or a scripture. It’s that imagination of a glorious society, made enforceable.

When Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and the others wrote the Constitution, they weren’t just setting up a government. They were imagining a civilization. Ambedkar called it Prabuddha Bharat — an Enlightened India — where a person’s caste, gender, religion, or birth wouldn’t determine how freely they could move, speak, or live. Liberty, equality, and fraternity weren’t supposed to just sit in the preamble looking nice. They were supposed to be alive. On the eve of the Constitution’s adoption, Ambedkar warned that India was walking into a life full of contradictions — political equality on paper, and deep social and economic inequality in daily life. He said if that contradiction were allowed to go unaddressed, the people suffering under it would eventually blow up the whole structure of political democracy. That warning is still hanging over us, mostly ignored. Caste wasn’t invented by the British — it existed long before them, and it outlived them too. Dalits and Adivasis still face discrimination in villages, in workplaces, in schools, and even in death — separate cremation grounds, separate wells, and separate seating still exist in parts of this country. People still get attacked over things as small as riding a horse to their own wedding, wearing certain …

author: Susan Price
title: Singapore’s unfinished anti-colonial struggle
content:
The dominant history of modern Singapore was meticulously constructed under the banner of the “Singapore Story”. By presenting the material interests of the ruling elite as the universal interests of the nation, the state narrative reduces the mass anti-imperialist movement of the mid-20th century into a fable; one wherein a heroic bourgeois leadership single-handedly navigates a vulnerable island state through the perils of communism to construct a prosperous capitalist metropolis.

In his six-part oral history series with Pintjin (PJ) Thum, Dr Poh Soo Kai, former student activist, co-founder of the People’s Action Party (PAP) and the Barisan Sosialis (Socialist Front) — and former political prisoner detained for nearly 17 years without trial — delivers a vital historical materialist counter-narrative.

In 36 minutes of personal testimony, Poh unpacks the class dynamics, state coercion, and geopolitical shake-ups that dismantled working-class power and shaped Singapore's transition into a disciplined capitalist state.

Poh begins by recalling how post-World War II Malayan households were adorned with portraits of Indonesia’s Sukarno, India’s Nehru and Gandhi, and China’s Chiang Kai-Shek, who were seen as regional anti-colonial leaders. The struggle in Singapore was bound to broader anti-imperialist movements across Malaya, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

Poh’s account of the 1954 Fajar Trial undermines the state’s origin myth, which positions the trial of eight members of the editorial board of Fajar (Dawn) — the University of Malaya Socialist Club’s newspaper — as Lee Kuan Yew’s (LKY’s) personal legal breakthrough.

[Editor’s note: Harry Lee Kwan Yew co-founded the PAP, was a barrister and opposition figure and became Singapore’s first Prime Minister in 1959.]

As president of the University of Malaya Socialist Club, Poh helped publish Fajar, an anti-colonial paper opposing the anti-communist South East Asian Treaty Organisation (SEATO) and foreign military bases. When the editorial board was charged with sedition, Queen’s Counsel DN Pritt arrived to lead the defense. Poh recounts Pritt greeting him warmly at the Dolphin Hotel before turning to LKY, who was acting as local junior counsel, and saying, “Harry, now you can go.”

Pritt dismissed LKY specifically to formulate an anti-colonial strategy directly with the student activists, recognising that the trial was a political battlefield rather than a legal technicality.

This moment symbolises the clash between the radical student movement and LKY’s legalism, and how official history later repackaged a left-wing victory as an LKY solo masterstroke.

As the PAP rose to power, internal contradictions between its left-wing mass base and moderate leadership erupted.

Poh recounts how the left wing consistently pushed for true self-determination, confronting PAP Chair Toh Chin Chye to issue a public statement supporting then-Chief Minister David Marshall’s 1956 call for internal self-rule — a move that infuriated LKY upon his return from London.

[Editor’s note: Marshall was appointed Chief Minister after contesting the 1955 election as a candidate for the Labour Front. After failing to secure self-rule, he resigned as Chief Minister in June 1956.]

Chief Minister Lim Yew Hock’s violent crackdowns on trade unions and Chinese school students from 1956 onward served a dual purpose: suppressing working-class organisation while allowing LKY to position himself as the sensible alternative acceptable to British imperial interests and local capital.

When dissident MPs and activists walked out to form the Barisan Sosialis in 1961, every PAP branch including LKY’s own Tanjong Pagar constituency defected to the new party. The PAP was left as a hollow electoral vessel without organic mass support.

To preempt an electoral defeat, the state deployed Operation Coldstore in February 1963. Officially framed as a security operation against a communist plot tied to the 1962 Brunei Revolt, Coldstore was a draconian political purge that sought to decapitate the political opposition, dismantle union leadership and ensure PAP hegemony.

The state weaponised identity politics to divide the multi-ethnic working-class by branding Chinese-educated labour leaders and Barisan Sosialis members as “Chinese chauvinists”. It replaced class-based solidarity with state-directed multiracialism that contained labour organising within non-threatening boundaries.

author: Alma Torlakovic
title: The gambling epidemic that Labor refuses to tackle
content:
Gambling is a public health crisis. Australians lose more money to gambling than any other nation on earth, per capita. Between March 2025 and March 2026, $36 billion was lost. Another way to put it is that a predatory industry manipulated people out of $36 billion in the space of just one year. The links between gambling and a plethora of issues, including harmful impacts on physical and mental health, relationships, work and education, are well established.  

That an industry can prey on some of the most vulnerable people in society should be a national scandal.

Let’s place this public health crisis in context.

Gambling companies sponsor major sporting events and are thus allowed prime-time advertising spots on TV. Their brands are plastered on players’ jerseys and stadiums, and they operate round-the-clock pokie rooms with almost no oversight or regulation. They are allowed to saturate advertising space on TV and online because the government refuses to implement even the most basic reforms, including those recommended by its own review.

The slimy gambling industry is a big donor to both political parties; Labor received $4.4 million between 2020-21 and 2024-25. At its recent national conference, the party allowed one of the big donors, hospitality and pokies giant Endeavor Group, to sponsor a party fundraiser on the side.

The gambling epidemic affects the poorest people the most. Existing issues such as financial stress, caused by an impossible housing and cost of living crisis, unemployment or mental health issues converge to make people more susceptible to taking gambling risks.

It’s no surprise that western Sydney is the centre of the gambling crisis. In October 2023, the Centre for Western Sydney published a research paper, “Luck of the draw? Inside western Sydney’s gambling harm epidemic”, which found that almost $9 million is lost to gambling in Sydney’s west every day. A third of the total gambling losses in Sydney happen in just three local government areas: Fairfield, Canterbury-Bankstown and Cumberland.

Almost everyone knows someone who’s been affected by gambling. Gambling companies engineer highly addictive technology to incite vulnerable individuals to gamble what little money they might have.

The pokie machine, an instrument of ruthless profiteering, is designed to entice a player to keep betting. Lights, sounds and big, flashy dollar signs promise an eventual jackpot to keep players mesmerised. The “feature”, also known as a “bonus play”, frequently pops up to keep them going. 

Importantly, the machine will never play a “losing sound”, even if a player is consistently losing. The visual and aural stimuli from a pokie machine trigger dopamine release in the brain at a rate of two to three hits per second, something that would normally occur only once per day. The intermittent rewards, however tiny, keep the player hooked. The unique jingles from a pokie machine end on a rising note, the effect being that it’s signalling an impending win.

Gambling companies have gone so far as to design pokie machines for a target audience, for example, using baby blue to target women and darker colours such as black and red to target young men.  

If it wasn’t infuriating enough that gambling companies prey on the poorest, working-class communities, this will be: in 2023-24, five of the largest online gambling companies extracted $5.4 billion from vulnerable punters, but paid $0.1 billion in company tax, with three of them paying nothing at all.

And gambling companies are hardly popular at the dinner table. In polling conducted by the Australia Institute, 81 percent of respondents supported banning gambling ads on social media and online, and 87 percent supported banning gambling ads during prime-time TV hours for families and children.

So why does Labor allow this to continue?

The donations are one thing. But more fundamentally, Labor is committed to a system that puts business profits above people. Labor doesn’t deserve the votes of working-class people in western Sydney. The party’s attitude to the gambling industry is just more proof of that.

author: AWSM
title: The anarchist case for abstentionism in elections
content:
The right to vote is seen by most as a necessary prerequisite for freedom across the world. People have fought and died for the right to vote in elections. Women across the world fought bitter battles for the right to vote. So why should anarchists question this as a right worth having?

The entire electoral show is designed to encourage us to believe that not only does our vote matter, but that it is the most important decision we could possibly make. Indeed, voting is held so sacred by many that the mere mention of not voting is enough to cause outrage. Pointing out that our vote makes no difference anyway, will see you accused of being apathetic, privileged, immature, and even being part of the alt-right!

But as noted anarchist Vernon Richards wrote,

“So long as we have capitalism and government, the job of anarchists is to fight both, and at the same time encourage people to take what steps they can to run their own lives.” [“Anarchists and Voting,” pp. 176–87, The Raven, No. 14, p. 179].

Electoralism ensures that a statist perspective becomes dominant. Everything is seen in terms of state intervention and following the decisions of the leaders, which has always proved deadly to encouraging a spirit of revolt, self-management, and self-help – the very keys to creating change in a society. Rather than being something other people discuss on behalf of working-class people, anarchists argue that politics should not be a specialised activity in the hands of the so-called experts (i.e., politicians) but instead lie in the hands of those directly affected by it in the process of participation, direct action, and self-management. Those that channel any “political” conclusions into electoral politics distort discussions into only what is possible within the current system. Given this, is it surprising that anarchists argue that the people “must organise their powers apart from and against the State?” [Bakunin, The Political Philosophy of Bakunin, p. 376].

Abstentionists get told, “If you don’t vote, you have no right to complain about the outcome,” but we consider the opposite to be true. It is those who have voted, who have agreed to the rules, and agreed to be governed by the winners who cannot complain. It is those who do not participate who have the right to complain about the outcome more than anyone else.

We get told that the reality is that voting does change things, but we can, and do, deny that. Voting attempts to provide the population with the illusion of change while in reality it reinforces the current system. A policy here and there may change, the faces may change, but the system of a wealthy minority ruling a poorer majority remains. People will continually be telling us that abstaining from voting will help the right-wing win the election, that it is better if the lesser evil wins. This may possibly be the case (although the argument is far from convincing), but why should we base our society on a compromise with evil? In fact, the “progressive” left wing party you vote for will often be ready to take the same actions as a right-wing government when it comes to imposing anti-working-class action upon us, (as we shall show later in this essay the state has a corrupting effect on those who enter politics with high principles). There should be a better way, and we say the dismantling of government, in all its existing and potential forms is that way.

Most of the left wing in Aotearoa, and quite a few people who claim to identify as anarchists, will support reformist parties in the upcoming election. You will hear them saying things like “vote Labour (or Green) without illusions,” or “vote Labour/Green but build a socialist alternative.” The slogans that these others may shout only reflect the idea that change can and should be brought about by a small number of elite politicians. Abstentionists do not say things like this. There are many problems with our electoral system of democracy, which we shall run through, but we must state that first and foremost, as anarchists, we see voting as against running contrary to our anti-statist and anti-hierarchy principles, and we see electoralism as contrary to our goals and practice. It reinforces the idea that society is divided into order-givers and order-takers. Famed French anarchist, Elisee Reclus, put it well when he said,

“Everything that can be said about the suffrage may be summed up in a sentence. To vote is to give up your own power. To elect a …

title: “There’s this sketchy Dutch black metal band touring Australia …”
content:
I was contacted a little while ago by somebody raising concerns about a couple of upcoming black metal gigs. Below is the text they sent.

There’s this sketchy Dutch black metal band, Helleruin, playing in Melbourne at the Northcote Social Club on September 11 and in Sydney at Crowbar on September 12.

Most of Helleruin’s records have been released on New Era Productions, which has put out a number of releases by fash black metal bands and which is run by Jasper Velzel, a NSBM and RAC musician. In addition, another project of Helleruin’s Carchost — Orewoet — is on the label Heidens Hart, which — along with releasing some far-right stuff — is owned by a former live guitarist of prominent fash band Graveland.

Moreover, a number of the local supporting acts have sketchy connections.

Order of Orias, one of two supports in Melbourne along with Petrol (see below), are on World Terror Committee, which releases fashy stuff and is owned by Sven Zimper, a member of prominent NSBM group Absurd.

Of the bands playing Sydney with Helleruin (Krvna, Pestilential Shadows, Destruktor, Vicissitude, Gravgöt, Grotesque Bliss, Petrol, Blasfemancia and Akhoth) at the ‘Call from the Grave’ festival:

Pestilential Shadows have released music on the Chinese label, GoatowaRex, who are very friendly to NSBM acts. Additionally, PS is part of a collective called Ordo Ater Anguis/Order of the Black Serpent, which includes numerous far right acts. Michael W Ford of Black Funeral appears to be a former Order of Nine Angles (09A) member in the United States who — after distancing himself from O9A — attempted to formulate a social Darwinist version of the Satanic Temple (lol), which coalesce around the Australian fash-friendly label, Dark Adversary. Indeed, one of the members of PS is also a member of Varw, a band on Dark Adversary. Further, Akhoth released a demo, ‘Storm of Pagan Fury’, on CD on Dark Adversary this year.

Grotesque Bliss are on Iron Bonehead which, along with the suspect name, appears to be run by a (if only barely) crypto-fascist.

Destruktor is on a label, Hells Headbangers, which has previously released and re-released stuff by Satanic Warmaster and Deströyer 666, including re-releasing Deströyer 666’s debut album, ‘Unchain the Wolves’, on a few different mediums over the last few years. Additionally, Inquisition had a few releases on Hells Headbangers after their lead singer (who is also a Satanist pedo) released openly fash music on fash label Satanic Skinhead Propaganda (a label which the Iron Bonehead guy sold in his old fash-friendly record store).

The most recent (2024) EP of Krvna, formally of PS, was released on Zazen Sounds, run by Greek nazi black metaller Acherontass of Αχέροντας (Krvna played guest guitar on their most recent album). For what it’s also worth, Third Eye Temple — the Polish label on which Krvna’s 2022 album was released — have released one split and re-issued an EP by Voidhanger, a side project of Polish far right black metallers, Infernal War.

Finally, Petrol were previously on a cancelled bill with Gurn. They also played a gig with Japanese band Abigail, who are signed to Nuclear Now Productions, a fash-friendly label linked to Iron Bonehead (similarly exposed by the nsbmboneheads blog linked above). In addition, Petrol played at Crowbar Sydney last year with Bolzer (see nsbmboneheads blog), who released all but their last record on Iron Bonehead. The other headliner was Portal, who have released lots of records on Hells Headbangers including, recently, a split with Blood of Kingu — a side-project of the Ukrainian ultra-nationalists from Drudkh — on the label in 2014.

author: Priya T.
title: Revisiting a Marxist classic: Hal Draper’s ‘Two Souls of Socialism’
content:
US socialist Hal Draper wrote

Two Souls of Socialism

in 1966 while working as a librarian at the University of California Berkeley. In the previous two years, student protests had turned the campus upside down. Radical left-wing politics was resurgent in the United States, after decades of stultifying McCarthyism.  

“For the first time in the history of the world”, Draper supposed, “very likely a majority of its people label themselves ‘socialist’ in one form or another; but there has never been a time when the label was less informative”. 

Among those carrying the socialist label were European social democrats who had abandoned challenging private property. The Soviet Union was at the height of its power, and Communist states modelled their economies on the one-party dictatorship, willingly or under the violent thumb of Russian imperialism. In the “Third World”, nationalist leaders from Gamal Abdel Nasser in Egypt to Kwame Nkrumah in Ghana adopted socialist rhetoric, while Mao Zedong in China and Che Guevara in Cuba won young disciples in the West. 

Then there were revolutionary socialists, like Draper, who insisted that socialism did not exist anywhere in the world, and that the regimes masquerading as socialist were dramatically unequal countries where workers had few democratic and political rights. Swimming against the stream, Draper wrote

Two Souls of Socialism

to salvage the authentic revolutionary tradition from the morass of Stalinism. He argued that working-class self-emancipation was the essence of socialism, and that the history of socialist thought could be understood through the competing visions of “socialism from below” and “socialism from above”. 

Socialist ideas of one sort or another have existed for a long time. Every society that has produced wealth and privilege for some, and deprivation and misery for many more, has had opponents. Political ideas calling for equality between peoples and freedom from oppression have repeatedly surfaced. So too has popular resistance, from slave uprisings in ancient Rome and peasant rebellions in medieval China to strikes and mass protests in modern capitalism. 

While “the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle”, as the

Communist Manifesto

 famously asserts in its opening, the content of socialist political thought has varied widely depending on the social class it is rooted in. 

Draper locates the origins of modern socialism in the radical political currents that proliferated following the French Revolution. Most eminent left-wing thinkers of this time were sympathetic to the plight of the labouring classes and believed that communism would lift the majority from oppression. However, by and large they did not conceive of the masses leading a socialist transformation of society. 

An archetype of “socialism from above” was the French revolutionary Babeuf, who believed that an enlightened minority that had risen above the intellectual and moral strangleholds of capitalism needed to seize state power in the interests of the majority. This was a conspiratorial vision of revolution “from above”, one that Draper summarised as being “frankly a dictatorship

over

the people—with very good intentions”. 

The “utopian” socialists arose soon after Babeuf and were path-breaking political thinkers. Draper highlights Robert Owen and Henri de Saint-Simon as socialists who advanced the first systematic critiques of early capitalism. They were, nonetheless, utopian as they dreamed up elaborate models of socialism and sought to procure resources from the propertied classes and the wealthy to impose their schemes onto the existing society. 

Owen sought rich financiers for establishing socialist communes. Saint-Simon did believe that popular struggle could exert powerful influence, but wanted to utilise it as what Draper calls a “battering ram”—a lever that could force the existing ruling class towards a fairer society, while leaving political and economic power in their hands. The utopian socialists advanced devastating critiques of inequality, and their dreams were radical. But their vision was nevertheless “socialism from above”, in that socialism was a blessing to be bestowed on the masses. 

Karl Marx began his political life where the utopian socialists left off, believing that workers would be the “heart” of a revolution while philosophers would be its “head”. Initially, Marx held to what Draper called the “illusion of the …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Two fossil states, one public bill
content:
Australia digs fossil fuels; Türkiye burns them. One exports coal, the other imports it.

Then came Woodside — a nine-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) deal, signed weeks before COP31 was awarded to Antalya. Two states, one fossil fuel relationship, one climate summit.

The partnership shows how both governments talk about climate finance and what they refuse to name.

Australia is hosting a leaders’ summit in Fiji in October and then Tuvalu. Why Tuvalu? Because the island is sinking and it makes a ready-made stage. But county’s leaders are not coming — Germany, Mexico and South Korea are sending ministers instead. The Pacific Resilience Facility has a target of $500 million; only $172 million has been pledged.

Had COP31 been held in Kaurna Yerta/Adelaide, the bill could have reached $2 billion.

The summits in Dubai and Baku were funded by petrostates — fossil fuel companies paid for access. Now it is Türkiye’s turn.

The answer to who pays is buried in the COP31 hosting agreement, passed by the Turkish Grand National Assembly on July 30. It lists many cost items but attaches no estimated price to any — a blank cheque.

The total is estimated to have already exceeded half a billion dollars — surpassing the cost of the NATO Summit held in Ankara just weeks earlier, and COP31 (Conference of Parties for the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change) has not even begun.

This money will come from the public. But this is not what the “climate finance” conversation is about.

The tourism revenue from the summit will flow to the big hotels. Türkiye’s Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Ersoy, is the co-founder of ETS Tour, one of Türkiye’s largest tour operators and Voyage Hotels.

The agreement passed with barely a question asked. Only one party filed a dissenting note. Five deputies voted against, 22 abstained; 38 opposition deputies voted in favour, while 115 opposition deputies did not turn up to vote at all.

The pattern is familiar; a 2019 law exempting thermal power plants from pollution filters passed in the same near-silence — until we published the attendance records.

Parliament had chosen silence; the public named it and the president was forced to veto the law he had just been handed. What is being named this time is different: the absence of 115 deputies.

Climate change is a capital transfer built on fossil fuels. What we need is an end to the destructive system the public is financing, not more finance to work within it.

Türkiye spent US$727 billion on fossil fuel imports between 2003 and 2022. Even 10% of that figure would constitute a major source of climate finance. But that money is already spent — feeding the fossil fuel system.

Asphalt, concrete, roads, buildings are fossil fuel systems too.

COP31 will be held on land built over farmland for the EXPO 2016 fair — used once then left idle — with a 150,000 square metre asphalt car park added for the occasion. They just are not named as climate policy.

The foundations of Türkiye’s largest climate-changing corporations came together in June to launch the “Philanthropy for Climate” initiative.

Who are the founding signatories? Koç Holding, which operates Türkiye’s largest oil refinery, Sabancı Holding, which owns Enerjisa’s coal and gas plants and Çimsa cement operations is a key player and TAV Airports, which operates Antalya Airport in the city hosting COP31.

They claim to be “taking responsibility for the climate”, but laundering it is a more accurate description.

What makes it worse is that environmental organisations, education and health bodies have signed on.

Sixteen organisations in Türkiye pushed back saying: “Those who are changing the climate cannot clear their own name”.

Other ecology and environment movements had no position. That silence gave Philanthropy for Climate exactly what it needed: civil society legitimacy.

“Climate finance” may be the most content-free phrase in the climate debate. Türkiye received billions of dollars of climate finance from the World Bank, among others, and its emissions kept rising.

The public money going to fossil fuel imports is another form of financing, but it will not appear on the agenda of climate negotiations.

A climate activist flying in from Australia for COP31 will land at TAV’s airport, stay in a hotel built by the minister’s company and sit in rooms where the “finance” being discussed will be none of the above.

This is not a COP problem; it is proof of exactly what COP is …

author: Luca Tavan
title: The case for socialist organisation
content:
You only need to look at the headlines over an average week in 2026 to see why we need to get rid of capitalism. Wildfires intensified by climate change are raging across Europe and

detonating

 buried WWII-era bombs and mines. Drought and economic disruption from war are combining to threaten the

world’s food supply

. Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz is seeking US approval to forcibly “

depopulate

” Gaza.  

The 21st century was meant to mark the final triumph of capitalism, when a civilised, democratic version of liberal democracy would spread across the globe, uplift billions and resolve the problems of poverty and war. But people born this century have only seen things go from bad to worse. 

No wonder the last decade has been characterised by explosive resistance movements involving millions, from France to Nepal. While Australia is relatively stable, there’s no shortage of discontent, especially among young people. Australia had some of the largest and most sustained protests against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, for example. And resistance has started to emerge to the rise of One Nation, with conservative commentator Rowan Dean recently whining about the anti-Hanson high school walkouts: “You’ve got these school kids linking Pauline Hanson, oligarchs, fascism ... linking that to billionaires ... It’s really dangerous, it’s really sinister, it’s radicalisation of our youth”. 

So the injustices of capitalism are not just accepted by everyone all the time. Resistance of various sorts has always been a feature of the system. But to be effective, this resistance needs a clear goal and understanding of the adversary it is up against. Socialism has, since even before Marx’s time, been this goal. It proposes to replace the rule of capital, and its drive to accumulate profit ahead of all else, with a society run democratically by the workers who make the things we all need and depend on to live. This can be achieved only by workers taking collective, democratic control of their workplaces and industries and completely destroying the rule of the bosses and their state. In his poem

In Praise of Communism

 the revolutionary German poet Bertolt Brecht called this “[t]he simple thing that’s hard to do”. 

Simple, because socialism is the rational alternative to the insanity of capitalism. Workers’ democracy could solve climate change by doing what capitalist governments refuse to: expropriating the fossil fuel companies and redirecting resources to renewable energy generation and expansion, regardless of whether it’s profitable. Military build-up and wars between capitalist states for control of markets, natural resources and trade routes would be immediately redundant in a society organised to meet human need rather than generate ever greater profit for the few. 

Hard to do, because the capitalist class possess immense social power and numerous defences to protect their rule, from repressive laws and armed police to the loyalty of “moderate” political leaders, who will always ultimately defend the system. The power of the capitalist class means they influence what workers think and can demoralise those who do want to fight back. To win socialism, then, we will need to build a force as powerful as the political and ideological institutions of the capitalist class.

Socialist organisation is key to this. First, it presents a coordinated ideological challenge to the ideas promoted by capitalist institutions, from the education system to the mass media, that are reinforced numerous ways in our everyday lives. A lot of this is simply creating confusion about how the system operates, obscuring the power and interests that underpin the norms or prerogatives of the system. 

Take the mainstream economics taught in universities: it’s essentially a religious dogma that exists to justify the rule of the rich. As Marxist economist Richard Wolff explains: “the vast majority of students walk away from their economic courses with little more than free-market ideology”. It can’t explain why the system perpetually spirals into crisis, or why a world built on such abundance still contains so much poverty and desperation. Wars, likewise, and the real considerations driving them, are rarely discussed candidly by those waging them. 

Marxist theory endeavours to explain how capitalism actually works: why inequality, economic crisis and war are built into the logic of the system, and not just the product of irrational behaviour or …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Nepal disaster a climate warning for COP31
content:
The disaster in Nepal, Tibet and China has been described as being like a “horror movie” — even by those in the midst of the catastrophe.

Just as the wildfires in Europe and the Black Summer bushfires in Australia, it is hard to imagine just how catastrophic these climate-fuelled events can be — until they happen — and even then, it is hard to get one’s head around.

But climate scientists have warned for decades that in an increasingly warming world — the result of human-induced activity — catastrophic events are hard to predict but they will happen.

Scientists have also warned for decades that tipping points — critical limits in the Earthʼs climate and planetary sub-systems (rainforests and ice sheets) where small additional changes can trigger major and potentially irreversible shifts that continue on their own — will be more frequent.

They have also pointed out the injustice associated with these disasters: countries that had the least to do with the problem are the worst affected. This is what we are seeing in Nepal.

The climate emergency — seen today in fires across Europe, the melting glaciers in the Himalayas and the developing El Niño in the Southern Ocean — is not new. But it is getting worse. Just as shocking as the catastrophic events themselves, is that those in power refuse to do anything to avert it.

This is where we need more focus. Once, the Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese told us that the climate emergency was the “greatest moral issue of our time”. Now, asked by reporters if the world has to take some collective responsibility for not doing enough on climate change, he said that “now’s the time … to focus … very much on people who are incredibly traumatised”.

The most useful way Australia could reassure people who are traumatised is by taking a proactive approach to this global problem, to which this country, a major coal and gas exporter, makes a significant contribution.

Albanese and several other ministers in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum last week were keen to play down climate in favour of “security”, including the Pacific Policing initiative, which involves Australia training new recruits to counter “transnational crime”. But the climate crisis is the most serious transnational crime of them all.

Even Palauan President Surangel Whipps, not renown for being outspoken on climate, said: “It is hard to overstate the depth of emotion for those of us living on the frontline after having fought so hard to put the 1.5 degree limit at the heart of the Paris Agreement … calls for greater ambition are no longer enough — we need to see an urgent and unprecedented increase in political will and investment in a climate safe future.”

A United Nations Environment Program report, released in September, warns that global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030. “There are no good outcomes in remaining above 1.5°C,” it said.

It said “potential tipping points” include irreversible changes to ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (the system of ocean currents that acts as a global conveyor belt carrying warm surface water north and cold deep water south) and the erasure of the Amazon rainforest. All these would lead to intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss and submersion of small island states and low-lying coastal cities.

It said warming up to or less than 3°C would mean glaciers could lose more than a quarter of their mass by 2100 and sea levels would rise by 12.5 centimetres. Apart from severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies, it would mean “crossing thresholds that become difficult or impossible to reverse on human timescales”.

There is debate among climate scientists, some of whom say the UN is underplaying the scale of the global warming disaster. Climate Brink said: “Most forecasts predict that 2027 will set records, with the global average temperature reaching levels we would not expect until the late 2030s”.

The Nepal disaster is a reminder that climate change is the greatest security threat of our time. Burning of fossil fuels, which leads to more trapped greenhouse gases, continues to contribute to the accumulation of energy in the Earth system that, in turn, leads to uninhabitable temperatures.

Australia, a co-host of the COP31 in Türkiye, will argue that it is on track to reach its 2030 target of cutting emissions by 43% below 2005 levels …

author: Zak Borzovoy
title: What we can learn from the Victorian school staff revolt
content:
A major revolt, in which socialists have played a crucial role, has shaken one of the biggest union branches in the country. In this year’s campaign for a new Victorian Government Schools Agreement, Victorian school staff rejected, not one, but two, offers from the state Labor government, in defiance of our own union leaders. Australian Education Union (AEU) members have now agreed to a third, revised, offer, bringing this chapter of rebellion to a close. 

Our defiance paid off. Each time we voted down an offer, the subsequent revised offer contained important improvements. These included pay rises for education support (ES) staff equal to those of teachers, having one less soul-crushing meeting per week after school, a promise to fund the work required for Disability Inclusion Profiles, a $2,000 pro-rata cash bonus (equivalent to back paying our first 3 percent pay rise to January for some workers), a 1 percent annual bonus for top-of-the-range staff and securing our previous reduction in face-to-face teaching hours into our agreement rather than a separate deed with an expiry date. The government has also felt obliged to commit publicly to properly funding schools according to the minimum standards in the Gonski plan. 

Importantly, the government didn’t just offer us more because we voted no to its first two offers, but because tens of thousands joined the two statewide strikes and mass rallies to show we were serious about winning our demands. These incredible actions also refuted many of the arguments our union leaders used to de-escalate the campaign, including that there was no appetite for strikes. It also helped focus attention on the government’s failure to deliver necessary funding to schools and school staff, which was a major problem for a weak government. 

But one of our most important wins has little to do with the detail of the concessions we’ve wrested from the government. It is that we have put rank-and-file revolt in support of real wage rises and workload relief back on the political map. In an all-too-rare example of the sort of action and organisation that is needed to revive and rebuild a decent union movement, our campaign is instructive and an inspiration to workers elsewhere and in other industries. 

The timid, class-collaborationist approach of our union leaders, which the campaign by Victorian school staff stands in sharp contrast to, is a major factor in the long-term decline of real wages, a trend that economist Greg Jericho has pointed out has gone alongside robust

corporate profits

.

In Victoria, Labor has colluded with our union leaders to keep workers’ expectations low. The AEU is no exception. When the AEU leaders agreed to Labor’s offer in May, which would have left education support staff with significantly lower pay rises than teachers and delivered no meaningful improvements to conditions, they parroted the government’s own spin and scaremongering to justify their capitulation. 

The union leadership called a strike for 24 March this year. The response was enormous, with more than 35,000 school staff and supporters jamming the streets of central Melbourne. But rather than build on this, the union’s leaders immediately declared that there was no point trying to get the government to budge from its existing position. We were told that the same government that’s spending

$1.6 billion on enforcing “Australia’s toughest bail laws”

 and more than

$60 million annually on handouts to fossil fuel companies

, according to research by the Australia Institute, couldn’t afford to invest more in our schools and educators. 

They even used the government’s neglect of public education and the resulting staffing shortage, to argue it wasn’t possible to address our burnout-inducing workloads with phased-in reductions to class sizes or face-to-face teaching hours. This is despite there being 34,000 registered teachers not currently working in schools, according to the education department’s 2024 Teacher Workforce Snapshot, many of whom will likely return only once workloads are reduced.

Rather than mobilise members in a serious campaign of strikes to pressure the government to concede our demands, the AEU leaders accepted the government’s position and pressured members to abandon ours. When making excuses for the government didn’t work, they fell back on scaremongering about the potential for arbitration or the possibility of a Liberal and One Nation coalition government coming to …

title: Bingöl'de KHK'lilerden çağrı: İhraçlar görevlerine iade edilsin
content:
Bingöl – Eğitim ve Bilim Emekçileri Sendikası (Eğitim-Sen) Bingöl Şubesi öncülüğünde Kanun Hükmünde Kararname (KHK) ile ihraç edilen kamu emekçileri için Kent Meydanı’nda açıklama yapıldı. Açıklamaya KHK’liler ve Demokratik Kurumlar Platformu temsilcileri de katıldı. "Hakikatler ihraç edilemez" ve "KHK’liler onurumuzdur" yazılı pankartlar ardından konuşan KHK’li öğretmen Mursel Bek, işlerini iyi yaptıkları için ihraç edildiklerini ifade ederek 10 yıldır sürdürdükleri mücadeleden vazgeçmeyeceklerini belirtti.

Bek’in ardından açıklama metnini okuyan KHK’li öğretmen İsmail Koç, 15 Temmuz darbe girişiminin ardından ilan edilen OHAL’in kısa sürede muhalif kamu emekçilerini tasfiye etmenin aracına dönüştüğünü söyledi. On binlerce kamu emekçisinin etkili bir soruşturma ve savunma hakkı tanınmadan ihraç edildiğini kaydeden Koç, insanlık dışı koşullarla baş başa bırakıldıklarını ifade etti. Sürecin bürokrasiye kurban edildiğini dile getiren Koç, 23 Ocak 2017’de kurulan OHAL İşlemleri İnceleme Komisyonu’nun emekçileri yıllarca beklettiğini ve kapandığı 22 Ocak 2023 tarihine kadar başvuruların büyük çoğunluğunu reddettiğini aktardı. KESK’li ihraçların önemli bir kısmında hukuki mücadelesinin hala sürdüğünü ekleyen Koç, bu mücadelenin sadece bireysel bir hak arayışı olmadığını, yürütülen direnişin hukukun üstünlüğü ve demokratik bir ülkenin geleceği için yapıldığını ifade etti. Türkiye’nin kronik sorunlarının çatışmayla değil barış, demokrasi ve eşitlik temelinde çözülebileceğini, KHK mağduriyetlerinin giderilmesinin de toplumsal barışın en önemli adımlarından biri olacağını belirtti.

Koç, açıklamanın sonunda hükümete seslenerek taleplerini şöyle sıraladı: “Mahkemeler üzerindeki siyasi baskılara son verilmesini, yargı süreçlerinin hızlandırılmasını, bekletilen dosyaların derhal sonuçlandırılmasını ve hakkında beraat, takipsizlik veya göreve dönüş kararı bulunan tüm kamu emekçilerinin derhal görevlerine iade edilmesini istiyoruz.”

Açıklama, atılan sloganlarının ardından sona erdi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Tierra del Fuego: siguen negociándose los detalles para la vuelta a la producción de Aires del Sur
content:
Trabajadores de Aires del Sur en Río Grande se encuentran definiendo los detalles finales para consolidar el regreso a la actividad productiva.


Esto se da luego de que levantaran formalmente la toma de la planta el 1 de septiembre de 2026, tras 188 días de permanencia en las instalaciones, a partir de la autorización de la Justicia para el arrendamiento del inmueble por un periodo inicial de seis meses a la firma Athuel Electrónica.


La firma prevé desembolsar un millón de dólares durante el próximo año para reacondicionar las instalaciones y recuperar la plena capacidad operativa de la planta. Además, se proyecta fabricar un lote de 40.000 unidades de aire acondicionado bajo un esquema de trabajo a fasón.


La Unión Obrera Metalúrgica (UOM), por su parte, conduce una mesa de negociación prioritaria con el objetivo de resolver los puntos pendientes antes del reinicio efectivo de las líneas. Actualmente se están discutiendo los esquemas salariales y las modalidades de contratación bajo la figura de locación de servicios.


El sindicato y los delegados señalaron que esta reactivación temporal representa «el 50% de la lucha», ya que el objetivo final durante este semestre es lograr la venta definitiva de la fábrica como unidad productiva, manteniendo a la totalidad de los empleados.


La empresa aprovechará el equipamiento industrial ya instalado para dar continuidad a su proyecto de sustitución de productos avalado por el Gobierno nacional. En ese sentido, funcionarios del Ministerio de Producción y Ambiente de Tierra del Fuego ya han recorrido la planta para constatar las tareas de puesta a punto mientras se terminan de destrabar cuestiones administrativas ante la Secretaría de Coordinación Productiva de la Nación.
